title: The Hangover Part II
intro: The Hangover Part II was released in 2011, directed again by Todd Phillips and written by Craig Mazin; it follows the three members of "The Wolfpack" from the first film as they wake up from another crazy night — this time, in Bangkok. The status of this film was in doubt due to a Frivolous Lawsuit over the use of Mike Tyson's tattoo by Helms, but Warner Bros. successfully got the lawsuit dismisse

tropes.name: Arc Words
tropes.html:
"Bangkok has him now" in relation to Teddy. Later becomes important when Stu realizes that Teddy is trapped inside their hotel's elevator, meaning that Bangkok - the city itself - has him.
Stu: "Why does everyone keep saying that?!"

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geography
tropes.html: The monastery in Chiang Mai that the elderly monk comes from would in reality be about 700 kilometres away from Bangkok in the north of Thailand, rather than merely a short bus ride, meaning it would have taken fourteen hours just to get there and back. And getting from the Krabi resort to Bangkok and back by speedboat — since the two locations are on the opposite coasts of Thailand — would require a 1,500-mile journey through the straits of Malacca via Singapore and would clearly be impossible for the group to do in the limited time frame.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Medicine
tropes.html:
• Stu's new tattoo looks like it's almost completely healed already, even though it was only applied a few hours before.
  • When Alan reveals how he inadvertently drugged his friends again, there is absolutely no way that a combination of muscle relaxers (most commonly Baclofen, Soma, & Flexeril) and ADHD medication (most commonly Adderall, Dexedrin, Ritalin, & Vyvanse) would have an amnesiac effect. The muscle relaxers alone by have made them loopy and pass out early, but not cause amnesia. And the amphetamine-based ADHD medication would not only have prevented any amnesiac effect, but they would've been so hyper-stimulated that they would've been in control of their faculties.

tropes.name: Black Comedy
tropes.html: Subverted with Phil and Stu's initial reaction being along the lines of Dude, Not Funny! to Alan using a plastic bottle to simulate an erection, but when a monkey starts nibbling on it, everybody bursts out laughing.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html:
• Phil's phone call to Tracy to tell her they've lost Teddy gets one.
    Phil: It happened again.
    Tracy: Seriously, what is wrong with you three?
  • When the guys wake up and realize that they had another wild night, their initial reactions provide several call backs to the waking up in the first film, such as Stu asking about his teeth after Phil and Alan's shocked reactions to his new tattoo; and Alan immediately being asked if he roofied them again; and once they realize Stu's future brother-in-law is missing, one of the first places they check for him is the roof.
  • Chow jumps out of an icebox and, once again, begins beating on the three guys in Part II. Thankfully this time he is clothed.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Bangkok makes for a grittier setting than Vegas. Not to mention the whole bit about the severed finger and transvestite strippers.

tropes.name: Dating What Daddy Hates
tropes.html: Stu marries a Thai girl named Lauren whose father is a very stereotypical strict Asian parent who makes no secret of his disdain for Stu. He emasculates Stu, compares him to tasteless rice porridge, and is all too ready to call off the wedding when the Wolfpack is running late. After Stu stands up for himself at the end, he grows to accept him.<!--* DisneyDeath: [[spoiler:Chow.]]--><!--* DrivesLikeCrazy: Chow during the chase scene.-->

tropes.name: "Eureka!" Moment
tropes.html: How Stu figures out where Teddy is.

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html: All the girls at the club turn out to be transsexuals; while they prominently display breasts, they also have the male package down there. Then Stu finds out what he did with one of them the night before.

tropes.name: Fingore
tropes.html: Teddy loses a finger (all in good fun though, as he was playing five-finger fillet with a bowie knife and after severing the finger on a misaimed thrust the group plays with the detached digit).

tropes.name: Full-Name Ultimatum
tropes.html: "Stuart Price! Get your ass back over here!"

tropes.name: Funny Background Event
tropes.html: After Alan runs the speedboat aground and it eventually comes to a stop to the side of the wedding, he can be seen dropping the anchor on dry land.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: Kingsley uses Teddy as insurance that the guys get Chow to complete their "business transaction". Then when the deal happens it turns out those guys don't actually have Ted, it was just a sting operation and Chow gets arrested.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html: Mike Tyson tells Stu that he should have his tattoo removed. As in, the exact same tattoo that Tyson has on his face.

tropes.name: I Don't Like You And You Don't Like Me
tropes.html: Stu's father-in-law-to-be says that he's never told Stu, but he doesn't like him. Stu sheepishly responds that he already knew that.<!--* {{Jerkass}}: Kingsley [[spoiler:although it's an act]] and Stu's father-in-law.-->

tropes.name: Karma Houdini
tropes.html:
• It turns out that, as opposed to the first film, Alan deliberately roofied everyone, even if he was only targeting Teddy, which really doesn't make it any better. Other than the others getting mad with him for about a minute, there are no repercussions.
  • And two counts for when Stu slept with Kimmy, a kathoey (transgender woman) sex worker. One since, as Stu was clearly wasted and couldn't give informed consent, Kimmy raped him. Two since, even though Stu was wasted, the incident is quickly brushed over and he goes on to marry his fiancee without telling her the truth, or even getting tested for a quite possible STD.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: "Is that Alan driving the speedboat?"

tropes.name: Major Injury Underreaction
tropes.html: Both Teddy and his family are ridiculously calm about the fact that he not only cut off his own finger, but that the guys irretrievably lost it in Bangkok, with no chance of getting it reattached. The guy is a talented musician and is also training to be a surgeon; while this isn't a definitive career destroying injury note at least not for an M.D. in general, only for someone who specifically wants to be a surgeon. Medical specialities are divided in surgical specialities, that need manual dexterity (surgeons (what Teddy originally wants to become), neurosurgeons, ENT's and OB-gyn's are considered this); and non-surgical specialties, in which manual dexterity is more irrelevant (internal medicine, neurologists, general practitioners and especially psychiatrists). Losing a finger might cut you off for careers in the surgical specialties, but you certainly can still have a brilliant career in the non-surgical M.D. specialties. Also, this injury actually won't affect Teddy's musical talent. The finger Teddy loses in on his right hand, which is the hand that holds the bow when he's playing cello (as seen when he's playing the cello before they go to Bangkok). Though he may have to get used to holding the bow with four fingers, he could most certainly still play cello or most instruments., it's certainly going to make the next few months fairly stressful as he learns to cope with a missing digit, let alone the fact that his wound might have gotten dangerously infected over the past twenty four hours. But nope; all he does is shrug. Wacky Bangkok.

tropes.name: Male Frontal Nudity
tropes.html:
• Soon after they wake up, the Wolfpack notice a bunch of sheets with a mysterious bulge poking out of them. A monkey suddenly touches it and it turns out to be Chow's penis.
  • When the sex workers of the club reveal they are transexual, a shot depicts them walking around naked with their packages out.

tropes.name: Mexican Standoff
tropes.html: Chow apparently always ends up in one of these. He met his wife at one.<!--* NotQuiteDead: [[spoiler:Chow.]]-->

tropes.name: Only a Flesh Wound
tropes.html: Phil is shot in the arm. Only grazes him and leads to 8 stitches, but he makes sure to point out that had the bullet gone a little to the left, it would've killed him.

tropes.name: The Password Is Always "Swordfish"
tropes.html:
The password to Chow's overseas bank account is Baloney1.
Chow: Well, it used to be just baloney, but then they started making you add number.
Kingsley: Fuckin' annoying...

tropes.name: Plot Armor
tropes.html: How Teddy survived in an elevator with no food or water and a cut off finger.

tropes.name: Pun
tropes.html: As the transexual prostitute puts it with her Unsettling Gender-Reveal, "This is Bangkok, not Bangcunt".

tropes.name: Raging Stiffie
tropes.html: Invoked by Alan when stuffing his water bottle under the monk's coat.<!-- * RapeAsComedy: Stu is raped by the transsexual hooker.-->

tropes.name: "The Reason You Suck" Speech
tropes.html: Lauren's (Stu's fiancee) father gives a speech at the rehearsal dinner that essentially amounts to him insulting Stu and comparing him to dull, flavorless rice. At the end of the film, Stu inverts this and gives a "The Reason I Don't Suck" Speech.

tropes.name: Recycled with a Gimmick
tropes.html: It's pretty much the same movie with the same main characters, except in Bangkok, and with a different groom missing.

tropes.name: "Shaggy Dog" Story
tropes.html: Played straighter in Part II than in Part I — Teddy was in the elevator on his way to get ice for his severed finger, when the power went out a minute after Phil and Alan woke up. If the trio had figured that out there and then before going back to the resort, they would've just needed to explain Stu's tattoo and get Teddy to a hospital, instead of getting dragged into Chow's dealings.

tropes.name: Sequel Goes Foreign
tropes.html: Part II takes place in Thailand and includes the characters lampshading the fact that the same circumstances happened in a foreign country.

tropes.name: Ship Out of Water
tropes.html: When they are late for the wedding, the protagonists save time by skipping the mooring and driving a boat straight onto land.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: One of that's pretty much Genius Bonus: one of the pictures in the end credits montage is inspired by a Pulitzer Prize-winning picture taken during the Vietnam War. Some liked it, but Roger Ebert was horrified. invoked

tropes.name: Strictly Formula
tropes.html: Part II is pretty much the same exact thing, but in Thailand.

tropes.name: Stylistic Suck
tropes.html: Mike Tyson's singing can only be described as this.

tropes.name: Trailers Always Spoil
tropes.html: TV ads that ran the week Part II was released featured heavily the "Time in a Bottle" elevator scene, so when Chow dies 30 minutes in, you're pretty sure it's not going to stick.

tropes.name: The Tyson Zone
tropes.html: The Trope Namer asks to see the photos of the Wolf Pack's wild night by saying "I'm Mike Tyson. Nothing surprises me." And he still reacts to the pictures with a cry of "Motherfuck!"

tropes.name: Unsettling Gender-Reveal
tropes.html: The group visits a brothel to look for clues about Teddy. One of the prostitutes tells Stu about how she slept with him last night, but then she includes strange details like how she let out sperm. She's actually transexual, and this is punctuated with Male Frontal Nudity. Stu is left in shambles and thinks he can't get married after knowing this traumatic experience.

tropes.name: The Voiceless
tropes.html: The elderly man in the wheelchair. At first they're confused as to why he doesn't speak, and why he's wearing Teddy's hoodienote The hoodie was given to the monk by Teddy the previous night when they were rioting at a bar, prompting the police to fire tear gas at them, so the elderly man wouldn't be subjected to it. Which also explains why he had all of Teddy's wallet contents on him, such as ID cards, but then they learn he's a monk who has taken a vow of silence, and not even the other monks would be able to get him to speak.

tropes.name: Zen Slap
tropes.html: When the main trio try to locate Stu's missing future brother-in-law Teddy, they seek answers in a temple full of monks who then proceed to beat the men with their staffs for talking during their deep meditation.

title: The Hangover Part III
intro: The Hangover Part III was released in 2013, in time for Memorial Day, directed by Phillips once again and again written by Mazin. In this film, the Wolfpack make their way back to Vegas, but this time, they're not just cleaning up their own mess; they're also trying to survive an angry rival of Chow (Ken Jeong) who wants them to find his enemy — or else.

tropes.name: Abbey Road Crossing
tropes.html: In the third film◊. No zebra crossing available, apparently.

tropes.name: Actionized Sequel
tropes.html: To the point that comedy is almost an afterthought.

tropes.name: Actor Allusion
tropes.html: When explaining everything to the group, Marshall (played by John Goodman) claims that Chow "fucked [him] in the ass", one of Walter Sobchak's famous lines.

tropes.name: And the Adventure Continues
tropes.html: The Stinger has Alan, Cassie, and Phil wake up in a trashed hotel room, hungover and confused the night after Alan & Cassie's wedding. Stu emerges from the bathroom with breast implants and Alan remembers that the wedding cake was a gift from Chow, who emerges from the next room naked, laughing and swinging a samurai sword.

tropes.name: Artifact Title
tropes.html: The Hangover: Part III ditches the set-up of the first two films, and doesn't have the Wolfpack retracing a wild night they can't remember until The Stinger.

tropes.name: Badass on Paper
tropes.html: Alan. He isn't the sharpest knife in the drawer, but when the search for Chow seems to have gone cold, he gives a Dumbass Has a Point moment that gets them back on track, inadvertently gets Marshall and his henchman killed, and pulls off a Go Through Me on Chow by standing in front of Phil and refusing to move, which saves their lives because Chow is unwilling to shoot Alan.

tropes.name: Bad Boss
tropes.html: Marshall calls Black Doug a moron when he tells the group he sold the wrong drugs to Alan in the first movie, and then kills him for having failed him.

tropes.name: Bedsheet Ladder
tropes.html: Off the side of Caesar's Palace.

tropes.name: Black Dude Dies First
tropes.html: Black Doug is shot and killed by Marshall.

tropes.name: Blofeld Ploy
tropes.html: Marshall seems to be about to shoot Doug, but shoots Black Doug instead.

tropes.name: Bond One-Liner
tropes.html: After Marshall and his men shoot into the trunk where they believe Chow is holed up: "End of conversation."

tropes.name: Bring My Brown Pants
tropes.html: Alan pisses his pants when Black Doug is killed by Marshall. Marshall gives him a pair of sweatpants to compensate.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html:
• Phil makes a joke about Stu getting tested for any disease from the face tattoo, though he is obviously making jokes about Stu's encounter with the hooker in Bangkok.
  • Before the third film ends, there is a shot of the Wolfpack walking together to Alan's wedding as they've done in the past.
  • In the first film, when Chow stomps on his satchel, Alan gets upset, claiming that there were Skittles in there. During the flashback at the liquor store, Alan can be seen buying Skittles along with alcohol.

tropes.name: Character Development
tropes.html: The underlying plot of this movie is that Alan is finally forced to grow up now that his father is gone and his family can no longer deal with his antics. The insanity he's put through while dealing with Chow, who he genuinely considers to be a friend, is what finally opens his eyes that he needs to change.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: In the first movie, when Stu was explaining to Black Doug that he gave Alan the roofies instead of ecstasy, he claimed someone named Marshall will get mad at him for it. Marshall shows up in Part III.

tropes.name: Color Blind Confusion
tropes.html: Chow being color blind means that he can't tell Stu which wire to cut when both are trying to disarm two parts of a security system at the same time.

tropes.name: Comically Missing the Point
tropes.html:
Alan does this quite a few times.
  • When scolding Alan at the start of the film, his father mentions that Alan is 40 years old and still lives at home, and needs to finally grow up. Alan points out that he's actually 42.
  • In a flashback to the events of the first film, Alan is shown approaching Black Doug to buy drugs from him, and casually addresses the latter with the N-Word. When Black Doug (naturally) gets hostile for this, Alan reassures him that he isn't an undercover cop, having no idea why Black Doug was actually mad at him.
  • Chow uses a miniature replica of his house, actually Marshall's, to illustrate his plan to break in and get the gold. After he explains the plan in full detail, Alan points out that they can't break into the house, because it's too small.

tropes.name: Comic Trio
tropes.html: Phil leads, Stu complains, and Alan goes along with it when not making things worse.

tropes.name: Covers Always Lie
tropes.html: The first teaser poster◊, parodying Harry Potter And The Deathly Hallows - Part 2, depicts Las Vegas on fire. The city is fine in the movie.

tropes.name: Creator Cameo
tropes.html: Director Todd Phillips briefly appears as a guy paying a prostitute while Chow parachutes by their hotel window.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: Part III is this to Part II (which was this to the original). Part III includes four onscreen human deaths (three of them murders), a plot involving Phil, Stu and Alan trying to drug Chow to deliver him to a gangster in return for Doug and a lot of animals dying in gruesome ways.

tropes.name: Dark Is Evil
tropes.html: Marshall, who has Black Doug as his head of security, is always seen wearing a pair of shades and has a black limo, which he allows the group to use to track down Chow after Chow steals Phil's minivan.

tropes.name: Didn't Think This Through
tropes.html:
• At the beginning of the film, Alan purchases a giraffe to keep as a pet. Already a ridiculous idea in itself, he then tries to transport it home himself in an open trailer attached to his car, taking a freeway that has low clearance bridges with no regard for whether the animal can fit under them. Sure enough, this results in the giraffe getting decapitated, which in turn causes a massive pile-up behind Alan that shuts down the freeway.
  • Chow parachuting out of his hotel room to escape from Phil and Alan. He lampshades it himself when he's about to land on top of the limo.
  • Alan lets Chow out of the limo's trunk, but doesn't think to take his gun away. He has to pull off a Go Through Me in order to stop Chow from trying to shoot Phil.

tropes.name: Dumbass Has a Point
tropes.html:
• Alan has one when they're trying to come up with a place they can catch Chow and drug him, saying they could use a movie theater. Phil says it's a great idea because they can use the darkness for cover in catching Chow.
  • Black Doug remarks that "Somebody's gotta pay" when Marshall reveals that the villa is his and Chow ripped him off and killed his guard dogs. Marshall says "He's right" and instead of shooting Doug as Black Doug thought he would do, shoots Black Doug instead.
  • When Phil remarks that he left his phone in the minivan, which Chow stole, Alan pipes up that he has a find my phone app, and Stu backs up Alan's point by saying they can track Chow down with the app, as if Chow stole the minivan and the phone is in it, it can lead them to Chow, which it does. In fact, without Alan's point, the film wouldn't have gone any further.

tropes.name: Evil Versus Evil
tropes.html: Marshall vs. Chow.

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Marshall acts like a gentleman, but in reality he's very threatening, manipulative and prone to killing others to get what he wants.

tropes.name: Genre Shift
tropes.html: The film heavily downplays the raunchy, comedic tone of its predecessors and plays out more like a straight crime thriller.

tropes.name: Go Through Me
tropes.html: Alan does this for Phil when Chow had his gun pointed at the latter. Since Chow considers Alan a friend, partly because he's the only one who wrote to him while in jail, and more importantly, opened the trunk and gave him his gun, thus allowing him to survive Marshall's attack, Chow ultimately relents and allows them to live.

tropes.name: Grand Finale
tropes.html: To hammer the point home, several of the movie posters just have "It Ends" for the tagline, except for the group poster, which has "The End", and the poster that homages Harry Potter, which has "It All Ends".

tropes.name: Headphones Equal Isolation
tropes.html: Part III has a shot of Alan, smugly listening to music through some headphones, as his father dies from a heart attack in the background.

tropes.name: The Heist
tropes.html: Part of the plot this time around, the Wolfpack has to locate Leslie and steal back $21 million worth of gold for another drug lord.

tropes.name: Hookers and Blow
tropes.html: Chow's hotel room in Caesar's Palace. We only sees flashes of it for the most part due to the strobe lights. Made awesome due to Black Sabbath being played in the background.

tropes.name: Impersonating an Officer
tropes.html: As seen in a flashback, Chow doing this sets the plot of the film in motion.

tropes.name: Large and in Charge
tropes.html: Marshall is definitely the one pulling the strings and is quite a bulky guy.

tropes.name: Low Clearance
tropes.html: The giraffe being decapitated on the highway and its head flying into an unsuspecting family's minivan. What the Hell, Hero?

tropes.name: Meaningful Background Event
tropes.html: Sid's heart attack in Part III, in the background of a shot focused on Alan listening to music through his headphones.

tropes.name: Meaningful Funeral
tropes.html: Played for laughs with Alan's angelic performance of Ave Maria at his dad's funeral.

tropes.name: Not Me This Time
tropes.html: After the Wolfgang wakes up from a third night they can't remember in The Stinger, Stu immediately blames Alan for drugging them. Only it was Chow this time.

tropes.name: Off with His Head!
tropes.html: The giraffe at the start of the film, courtesy of a bridge on the highway.

tropes.name: Only One Name
tropes.html: Marshall. We don't find out if this is his first name or surname, or hear his full name. We don't find out Black Doug's full name either.

tropes.name: The Password Is Always "Swordfish"
tropes.html: Alan's changed his phone's password to "heyphil", to Phil's confusion.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html: After Marshall kills Black Doug, he gives Alan a spare pair of sweatpants after he had wet himself. Understanding how scary the moment was.

tropes.name: Plot-Triggering Death
tropes.html: The third film starts with Alan going off his meds after his father passes away. His friends offer to take him to rehab, but the main story ambushes them en route.

tropes.name: Prison Riot
tropes.html: Chow starts one so the guards would be distracted as he escaped.

tropes.name: Rule of Pool
tropes.html: When Marshall kills Black Doug for having failed him, his corpse is left floating in the pool.

tropes.name: Rule of Three
tropes.html: Todd Phillips did this to finish the series out as a trilogy.

tropes.name: Scary Black Man
tropes.html: Subverted with Black Doug. He tries to come across as this due to being associated with Marshall, but he's really incompetent. He sold the wrong drugs to Alan in the first film and his ideas for security at Marshall's villa are bypassed by Chow, so Marshall kills him.

tropes.name: Screw This, I'm Outta Here
tropes.html:
• Subverted. Alan tries running away from the minivan when Stu, Doug and Phil are captured. One of the henchmen catches up to him and captures him too.
  • Played straight when Chow locks Phil, Stu and Alan in the villa's basement, reactivates the alarm, steals the gold and Phil's minivan, leaving them to their fate.

tropes.name: Self-Serving Memory
tropes.html: Alan's father berates him as a total loser and screw-up who has to grow up or he's cut off. At the man's funeral, Alan recalls his father's words as being "I love you, son. Don't ever change." It's clear he truly believes it.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
This poster◊ spoofs the face-off◊ between a certain Evil Sorcerer and his boy wizard nemesis.
  • Chow's prison escape is pretty obvious.

tropes.name: Staging an Intervention
tropes.html: This is the inciting incident.

tropes.name: The Stinger
tropes.html: The Wolfpack wakes up after yet another wild night they can't remember.

tropes.name: Sudden Sequel Death Syndrome
tropes.html: This happens to Alan's dad, Sid Garner, courtesy of Alan giving him a heart attack when he hauls a giraffe onto a highway with his car, only to have it graphically decapitated by an overpass, and especially because of Alan's nonchalant reaction to what his dad had to do in order to fix the mess. This also ends up sending the entire plot into motion.

tropes.name: Take That, Critics!
tropes.html: The Stinger is one to everyone who complained how unbelievable it was that the Wolfpack had a second wild night they couldn't remember in Part II.

tropes.name: Villain Has a Point
tropes.html: Leslie Chow, as Marshall puts it, is madness. His first move upon having Chow on the backfoot and locked in the trunk is to kill him. This entire film has shown us that Chow is a very chaotic person and can't be trusted so this is definitely the smart move.

tropes.name: Villainous Rescue
tropes.html:
Happens twice to the Wolfpack in this film:
  • The first is when they're bailed out of a Mexican police station. By Marshall, whose house they had just broken into.
  • The second time, they're rescued by Chow, whom Alan helped free and gave him access to his handgun. When Marshall finds out Chow wasn't in the trunk of the limo, he was prepared to shoot them, until Chow pops up from the limo top, and shoots him and his bodyguard in the head.

tropes.name: Wire Dilemma
tropes.html: Stu and Chow have to cut the same wire on two panels of a security system at the same time to disable it, but Chow is colorblind and dyslexic.

tropes.name: You Have GOT to Be Kidding Me!
tropes.html: Crosses over with Wire Dilemma above. When Chow reveals he's dyslexic as well as colorblind, you can hear this trope in Stu's exasperated "What. The Fuck?!"

tropes.name: You Have Outlived Your Usefulness
tropes.html:
A couple of examples:
  • Chow does this to the Wolfpack when they help him steal the gold from the Mexican villa. He then proceeds to reactivate the alarm, and then snaps the necks of the sleeping guard dogs before leaving them to their fate.
  • Marshall does this to black Doug after he frees the Wolfpack from the Mexican authorities. He claims that his head of security isn't doing his job if a bunch of guys managed to break into the villa and steal the gold.

title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
original_title: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me
intro: Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me is a 1999 American spy comedy film starring Mike Myers and directed by Jay Roach. It is the second installment in the Austin Powers film series. The film stars Myers, Heather Graham, Michael York, Robert Wagner, Seth Green, Mindy Sterling, Rob Lowe, and Elizabeth Hurley. Dr. Evil steals Austin's "mojo", forcing Austin to travel back to the 1960s to restore his

tropes.name: Advertised Extra
tropes.html: Certain trailers made it seem like Robin Swallows was going to play a significant role. In actuality, she has less than five minutes of screen time.

tropes.name: Ain't Too Proud to Beg
tropes.html: Austin tearfully pleads "No more!" after Mini Me pummels him on the moon.

tropes.name: Anachronism Stew
tropes.html: Elvis Costello makes an appearance singing for Austin and Felicity, but the scene in question took place in 1969, which meant he would've only been fifteen years old (and looked much older than that). This is played for laughs like everything else. Burt Bacharach and Woody Harrelson also look to be as old as they were in 1999 in 1969.

tropes.name: Anguished Declaration of Love
tropes.html: When Austin fails to save Felicity in the first run of events, he quietly whispers "I love you, Felicity."

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html: Upon being asked if he's happy, Fat Bastard breaks down in tears when he admits he's not. Unusually for this series, it's played relatively straight until he lets out a fart.

tropes.name: Artistic Licence
tropes.html:
To British viewers at least, the "newspaper" Austin reads in the space station is clearly a mockup designed by somebody who has never seen the real paper:
  • Although the paper is nicknamed "the London Times", to distinguish it from similarly-named papers such as the New York Times, its official name (the one on the masthead) is "The Times".
  • The masthead design is totally wrong.
  • In particular, the masthead (like the rest of the paper) is in Times New Roman, not the Fraktur typeface used. (Many British papers have moved away from the Fraktur tradition.)

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
• Historically, the U.S. president in 1969 was, of course, Richard Nixon. The film just ignores this and instead features a generic fictional president.
  • Dr. Evil's demand for 100 billion dollars is treated as absurd by the government because "that amount of money doesn't even exist" in 1969. In reality, that amount of money did exist in 1969. The federal budget for spending alone was nearly double that at $182.8 billion.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Military
tropes.html: Fat Bastard's OIC is wearing a lance sergeant's forage cap rather than one appropriate to his actual rank of colonel.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: When the President wants to launch nuclear missiles at the moon, he is stopped by his military advisor who asks if he's suggesting they blow up the moon. All the nuclear warheads in the world in 1969 wouldn't even be able to do that. Even if every single nuclear weapon created by NATO and the Warsaw Pact during the Cold War were launched at the moon, a total of over 60'000 nuclear warheads, they wouldn't even crack the surface.

tropes.name: Ass Shove
tropes.html: After charming Fat Bastard into bed, Felicity plants a tracking device on him by shoving it up his buttock cleavage. Fat Bastard thinks she's being "frisky".

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html:
• While in his pad at 1969, Austin stands beside a woman, and suddenly says "Get your hands off my Heinie, baby!" The woman moves her hand into shot, revealing that she's holding a Heineken beer.
  • After Austin finds out that Felicity got close enough to plant a tracking device on Fat Bastard by having sex with him, he asks her how she could do it. Felicity responds that it's her job to do morally ambiguous things. Then, Austin clarifies that he was asking how she could physically do it due to how big Fat Bastard is.

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch Comment
tropes.html:
Invoked by Felicity.
Felicity: Well, Austin, I think this time you may have finally met your match.
Austin: Oh no, baby. I've beaten Dr. Evil before, and I'll beat him again.
Felicity: (smirks) I was talking about me.

tropes.name: Batman Can Breathe in Space
tropes.html: Mini-Me is ejected out into space unprotected, and survives completely unharmed (though Dr. Evil thinks this warrants a flu shot).

tropes.name: Between My Legs
tropes.html: Mini-Me is briefly framed between Austin's legs as he charges over to bite his opponent in the crotch.

tropes.name: Big Little Man
tropes.html: Mini-Me's introduction. Upon the announcement that Dr. Evil has been cloned, a regular-sized silhouette of him is outside the door. The door open revealing that said clone is tiny.

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: "As the French would say, it has a certain... I don't know what." The phrase je ne sais quoi, a popular term borrowed from French to describe some indescribable aspect of something, literally translates to 'I don't know what'.

tropes.name: Blatant Lies
tropes.html: When Basil tells Felicity not to get too close to Austin, she retorts that her interest in this case is "purely professional" - despite the fact that she had just tried to sleep with Austin.

tropes.name: Blow Gun
tropes.html: Mini-Me shuts down Austin and Felicity's interrogation by using one of these to hit Mustafa in the neck with a poison dart.

tropes.name: British Royal Guards
tropes.html: Has a montage where Austin and Felicity goad a royal guard into participating in a Motionless Makeover.

tropes.name: Bulletproof Human Shield
tropes.html:
Robin Swallows can protect Austin from machine gun fire and a bazooka rocket.
Austin: Why Won't You Die?!

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html: Scott suggests that Dr. Evil just go back in time and kill Austin "while he's sitting on the crapper", a nod to Paddy O'Brien's assassination attempt on Austin in the first film.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Rebecca Romijn As Herself, and Kristen Johnston as Dr. Evil's spy Ivana Humpalot, appear as models in the beginning. The latter Austin tries to bed, only to reveal her allegiance.

tropes.name: Captain Obvious
tropes.html: Fat Bastard, after cutting one: "Sorry. I farted."

tropes.name: Censored Title
tropes.html: The movie was often advertised in Britain as "The Spy Who...", leaving out the last two words. In Britain, "shag" is a much dirtier word than it is in North America. Averted or inverted (depending on whether the new title is considered more offensive than the original) in Norway, however, where the title translated as The Spy Who Spermed Me.

tropes.name: Cluster F-Bomb
tropes.html: The Jerry Springer scene. All censored, of course.

tropes.name: Comic Sutra
tropes.html: The opening scene shows that Austin apparently published his own version of the Kama Sutra, and states that he and Vanessa are only halfway through it on their honeymoon.

tropes.name: Contrasting Replacement Character
tropes.html: Felicity is this to Vanessa Kensington, Austin's partner and love interest from the first movie. Vanessa is British, while Felicity is American. Vanessa was a modern woman of the 90s, while Felicity is from the same time period as Austin. While it took some time for Vanessa to warm up to Austin, Felicity is clearly enamored of Austin the moment they meet owing primarily to them being from the same time period where Austin was considered a sex symbol. And finally, while Vanessa Kensington had a rather normal name, Felicity's name is quite unusual.

tropes.name: Contrived Coincidence
tropes.html: British Intelligence just so happen to have developed their own time machine, allowing Austin to follow Dr. Evil back to the 60s.

tropes.name: Convection, Schmonvection
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's hollowed-out volcano lair, in particular the Lava Pit Death Trap that only burns you if you fall in.

tropes.name: Conveniently Empty Roads
tropes.html: Austin and Felicity are chased down the countryside by one of Dr. Evil's assassins. Not only do they not pass a single other car during the chase, but no one drives by as they interrogate the assassin.

tropes.name: *Cough* Snark *Cough*
tropes.html: Scott mocks Dr. Evil saying his laser will turn the moon into what he calls a "death star" by pretending to cough in order to hide him saying "Ripoff!"

tropes.name: Covert Pervert
tropes.html: When Austin's arrival in the past causes a women to faint, a man catches her... and proceeds to gawk at her figure. This same fellow also openly stares at Felicity's chest when she pulls him in for a dance.

tropes.name: Delayed Ripple Effect
tropes.html: While Fat Bastard steals Austin's mojo in 1969, Austin only realizes he's lost it in 1999.

tropes.name: Distaff Counterpart
tropes.html: In many ways, Felicity is the female equivalent to Austin. With Austin in his currently diminished state, meeting someone who is more like him than he is at the moment further affects his self-confidence (especially when he forces himself to turn down Felicity's offer of sex).

tropes.name: Distracted by My Own Sexy
tropes.html:
When going back in time to ten minutes ago, Austin interacts with his past self who compliment how "sexy" they both look, confusing everyone in the room.
Dr. Evil: Alright, this is ri-goddamn-diculous, kill 'em both!

tropes.name: Does This Remind You of Anything?
tropes.html:
Dr. Evil's rocket has a long, slender fuselage and two spherical fuel tanks near the thruster, thereby making it look like a giant flying—
Pilot 1: Dick, look out of starboard!
Pilot 2: Oh, my God, that looks like a huge—
Birdwatcher 1: Pecker!
Birdwatcher 2: Oh, where?
Birdwatcher 1: Wait, that's not a woodpecker! That looks like somebody's—
Sergeant: PRIVATES, WE HAVE REPORTS OF AN UNIDENTIFIED FLYING OBJECT! IT HAS A LONG SMOOTH SHAFT, COMPLETE WITH—
Umpire: TWO BALLS! Hey, what's that? It looks like an enormous—
Chinese Teacher: Wang, pay attention!
Wang: I was distracted by the enormous flying—
Guitarist: Willie, what's that?
Willie Nelson: Well, that looks like a huge—
Colonel: Johnson?
Radar Operator: Yes, sir?
Colonel: Get on the horn to British Intelligence and let them know about this.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Music
tropes.html: Felicity makes her presence known to Austin by dancing provocatively to "American Woman" by The Guess Who.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Standards
tropes.html:
• Played both ways and for levity during The Jerry Springer Show sequence. Even the Neo-Nazi and the Klansman think Dr. Evil's a freak (and the latter calls him out as such). Dr. Evil, for his part, becomes angry at the Klansman's verbal disparaging of Scott. Their relationship may be strained, but even Dr. Evil's not going to let anyone talk to his own son that way (and attacks the Klansman in retaliation).
  • Dr. Evil then invokes it again later when Fat Bastard mocks Austin after learning Felicity slept with the Scotsman. As much as Dr. Evil enjoys seeing Austin in any kind of agony, having to also imagine Fat Bastard naked is just too gross.

tropes.name: Eye Scream
tropes.html: Mini-Me jams his thumbs into Austin's eyes during their fight on the moon.

tropes.name: Failed a Spot Check
tropes.html: When the Fembot Vanessa unleashes her "machine gun jubblies", Austin playfully wonders how he could have missed those during their lovemaking. The Fembot coldly responds "Perhaps next time you should try foreplay!"

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html: Naked Fat Bastard. Send the Brain Bleach! Dr. Evil even lampshades this in-universe.

tropes.name: Fantastic Plagiarism
tropes.html: While he's in the past, Dr. Evil claims credit for various contemporary pop cultural fads, such as claiming "One of Us" was a song he invented. Of course, Scott starts calling him out when he comes back.

tropes.name: Faux Paw
tropes.html: When Austin first sees Felicity, He licks his hand and grooms himself like a cat, in some kind of enticement ritual. He follows up by pushing his "paws" forward as he makes his way toward Felicity.

tropes.name: Flipping the Bird
tropes.html: Mini-Me often uses this gesture to mock others.

tropes.name: Flirting Under Fire
tropes.html: Austin and Felicity have a tender moment... while standing in a laughably pathetic Death Trap.

tropes.name: Forced Dance Partner
tropes.html:
Austin is drawn to the beautiful and flirty Felicity Shagwell. Before he can embrace her, Robin Swallows suddenly pops up inbetween them, pushing Austin across the dance floor and away from Felicity, to Austin's distress.
Austin: (reaches for Felicity) I want! I want!!

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: Immediately after Frau tells Dr. Evil that she's late, Scott comes through the time portal and joins them. In The Stinger, we learn that he's not a test tube baby, but Dr. Evil and Frau's love child.

tropes.name: A Glass in the Hand
tropes.html: Vanessa in the beginning smashes a champagne bottle in her hand.

tropes.name: GPS Evidence
tropes.html: The heroes are able to find the location of Dr. Evil's volcano lair by analyzing Fat Bastard's stool sample, discovering traces of a rare vegetable that only grows on one island in the entire world.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: Mini-Me first kicks, then bites Austin in the crotch during their fight.

tropes.name: Hand Signals
tropes.html: Felicity Shagwell uses these to tell her agents to interfere with Robin Spitz Swallows.

tropes.name: Hand Wave
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's new volcano lair is stated to have been built after past Number Two received a "memo from the future".

tropes.name: Happy Ending Override
tropes.html: The film opens on Austin and Vanessa's honeymoon, whereupon Vanessa reveals herself as a Fembot and self destructs.

tropes.name: Head-Turning Beauty
tropes.html: Felicity catches Austin's eye from across the room, and quickly gains the attention of a couple of other men on her way over to him.

tropes.name: Held Gaze
tropes.html: In her first scene, Felicity locks eyes with Austin from across the room, and keeps looking at him even as she dances with two other guys.

tropes.name: Heroic BSoD
tropes.html: Austin falls into depression after forcing himself to reject Felicity's advances.

tropes.name: Heroic Seductress
tropes.html: Felicity charms Fat Bastard into bed with her so she can plant a tracking device on him.

tropes.name: High-Heel–Face Turn
tropes.html: Ivana Humpalot was sent to kill Austin, but she ends up confessing and sleeping with him instead, simply unable to resist him.

tropes.name: Hoist Hero over Head
tropes.html: Mini-Me lifts Austin up easily (in spite of his small stature), spins him around, then throws him across the corridor.

tropes.name: Hoist by His Own Petard
tropes.html: Mini-Me dominates Austin during their fight - up until the point where he crawls into Austin's spacesuit through the hole he tore in it. This allows Austin to trap him in the back and expel him into space via a "lunar waste" disposal unit.

tropes.name: Hurricane of Euphemisms
tropes.html:
Two scenes are used to describe what Dr. Evil's rocket resembles, including one at the end where he escapes in his flying—
Teacher: Penis! The male reproductive organ. Also known as "tallywacker", "schlong", or—
Father: Wiener? Anybody want another wiener?
Son: Dad, what's that?
Father: I don't know, son, but it has great big—
Vendor: Nuts! Hot salty nuts! Who wants some?! Lord almighty!
Woman: That looks just like my husband's—
Carnival Barker: One-eyed monster! Step right up and see the one-eyed monster!
Cyclops: Rawr! Hey, what's that? It looks like a—
Fan: Woody? Woody Harrelson? Can I have your autograph?
Woody Harrelson: Sure. Oh, my Lord! Look at that thing!
Fan: It's so huge!
Woody Harrelson: I've seen bigger. That's—
Dr. Evil: [putting a syringe into Mini-Me] Just a little prick.

tropes.name: Hypocritical Humor
tropes.html: After Austin escapes two assassination attempts in a row, Dr. Evil voices his disappointment, claiming that he is "the man who will maintain the dignity of this evil organization"... while driving around in a scooter (with Mini-Me repeatedly honking the horn).

tropes.name: I Ate WHAT?!
tropes.html:
Austin drinks Fat Bastard's stool sample, thinking it is coffee.
Austin: This coffee smells like shit.
Basil: It is shit, Austin.
Austin: Oh, good, then it's not just me. [drinks more] It's a bit nutty.

tropes.name: I'm Mr. [Future Pop Culture Reference]
tropes.html: Dr. Evil uses footage from the film Independence Day to frighten the president and others into thinking the White House is being attacked. But tells him that's what's gonna happen. He calls his moon laser the Death Star and the task of assembling it The Alan Parsons Project. Having gone back to 1969, however, only Scott realizes the idiocy.

tropes.name: Implacable Man
tropes.html: Played for laughs with assassin Robin Spitz-Swallows: she survives a knife in the back, a dozen bullets in the back, a shot from a bazooka in the face, and a ridiculously high fall out of a window with Austin landing on top of her. A spot of Lampshade Hanging occurs when Austin cries "Why won't you die?!" A deleted scene shows that he keeps her in the trunk of his car to deflect gunfire.

tropes.name: Impostor All Along
tropes.html: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery, ends with Austin marrying Vanessa. This film opens with the revelation that Vanessa is a Fembot. Vanessa was clearly a real person that existed, because she talks to her mother in the first film. It is unclear when the switch happened, though Austin doesn't seem to care, as the moment he's disposed of the Fembot, he's happy to be a bachelor again.

tropes.name: Improbable Aiming Skills
tropes.html: Towards the end, Austin fires fewer shots from his handgun than the number of henchmen he hits.

tropes.name: Inelegant Blubbering
tropes.html: Austin openly weeps after the first phase of Mini-Me's attack.

tropes.name: Inflation Negation
tropes.html: Inverted. Dr. Evil's 1969 ransom of one hundred billion dollars doesn't even exist yet.

tropes.name: Instant Seduction
tropes.html: Upon imbibing some of the stolen mojo, Dr. Evil immediately manages to charm Frau.

tropes.name: Intangible Theft
tropes.html: Fat Bastard steals Austin Powers' "mojo" (his libido and sexual prowess) for his arch-nemesis Dr. Evil. It's visualized as a red liquid with little male symbols floating in it.

tropes.name: Intimate Lotion Application
tropes.html: Felicity asks Austin to give her a Massage of Love, which first involves rubbing her back with scented oils. Since Austin has recently lost his mojo (the part of him that makes him so confident and skilled with women), he approaches the act with awkwardness and nervousness, and when she shows her bare back to him he ends up squeezing the bottle so hard the oil spills out.

tropes.name: Island Base
tropes.html: One of Doctor Evil's Evil Lairs.

tropes.name: I Surrender, Suckers!
tropes.html: During their fight in Dr. Evil's moon base, Mini-Me goves Austin the Peace sign, indicating he doesn't want to fight anymore. Austin accepts, only for Mini-Me to attack him while his guard is down.

tropes.name: It's Personal
tropes.html: Both Dr. Evil and Austin say this this in reference to how Dr. Evil's stolen Austin's mojo.

tropes.name: It Was with You All Along
tropes.html: Austin despairs after his mojo is destroyed, believing he's "useless" without it. Felicity points out that he actually had it with him all along, as he was still able to save the world from Dr. Evil.

tropes.name: Jaw Drop
tropes.html:
• The first guy Felicity dances with stares at her chest in slack-jawed awe.
  • Austin's jaw drops with surprise and lust when Felicity effortlessly counters his attempts at flirting, and again when he sees her dressed up in his pad.

tropes.name: Jump Scare
tropes.html: Mini Me pops up in front of Austin, making a yell, as the Moon fight begins.

tropes.name: Lame Comeback
tropes.html:
When Fat Bastard suggests that he and Felicity could have "another go", Austin retaliates rather feebly:
Austin: Shut your mouth, you bastard! ...Who is fat.

tropes.name: Lava Is Boiling Kool-Aid
tropes.html: Though Convection, Schmonvection is played straight, this trope is surprisingly averted. Objects (and people) which fall into the lava do not sink to the bottom, and at no point does the lava "flow".

tropes.name: Leno Device
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's return is announced to the world via...him and Scott appearing on The Jerry Springer Show.

tropes.name: Literalist Snarking
tropes.html:
• Vanessa asks Austin if he smokes after sex. Austin's response? "I don't know, baby. I never look!"
  • Another example is from Austin and Felicity's first meeting.
    Austin: Those are skintight. How do you get into those pants, baby?
    Felicity: You can start by buying me a drink.

tropes.name: The Loins Sleep Tonight
tropes.html: Austin, while in the middle of sex with Dr. Evil's spy Ivana Humpalot, suddenly loses his erection in 1999 when his mojo (libido/sex drive/virility) is stolen from his cryogenically frozen body in 1969. He then travels back to the Swingin' Sixties to reclaim his mojo and cure his erectile dysfunction. His desire to get his groove back is only heightened when the sexy spy/hippie Felicity Shagwell comes his way. With both wanting to shag each other, Felicity increases the swinger's desire to cure his impotency and get his mojo back from Dr. Evil so Austin and Felicity can finally do the horizontal tango.

tropes.name: Marshmallow Hell
tropes.html:
While scoping out Dr. Evil's headquarters, Austin is accidentally pulled down into Felicity's breasts.
Austin: Hello, mummy. Mummy, can I have some chocolates? I want some Mars bars! Don't smack my bottom, mummy...

tropes.name: Mirror-Cracking Ugly
tropes.html: Upon travelling back to 1969, Austin glances in his car's rear view mirror and sees that his teeth have returned to their original unkempt state - with the mirror cracking a second later.

tropes.name: Motionless Makeover
tropes.html: Part of Austin and Felicity's teasing of the beefeater involves them exchanging clothes with him in a series of quick shots.

tropes.name: MST3K Mantra
tropes.html: Invoked and lampshaded, when Austin has some issues with temporal causality. Basil Exposition tells him to just relax and try to enjoy it, then looks directly at the camera and tells the audience to do the same.

tropes.name: Naked People Are Funny
tropes.html: The opening credits play over a scene wherein Austin decides to celebrate his newfound singleness by taking a stroll through the hotel in the buff, his naughty parts concealed by various objects.

tropes.name: Never the Selves Shall Meet
tropes.html:
Averted, when Austin not only interacts with a ten-minute-younger version of himself, but the two of them apparently wind up engaging in a three-way with Felicity Shagwell.
Austin Powers: Technically it's not cheating, baby!

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: An early trailer made it seem like Robin Swallows had a larger role then she actually did.

tropes.name: No-Holds-Barred Beatdown
tropes.html: Mini-Me inflicts a brutal assault upon Austin, enough that Austin at one point tearfully pleads "No more!"

tropes.name: Not Actually the Ultimate Question
tropes.html:
When Austin asks Felicity how she could sleep with Fat Bastard, she tells him she was only doing her job. Austin replies that he meant that literally, as Fat Bastard is so fat that the idea of him even being able to have sex seems physically impossible.
Austin: The man's so fat, the sheer mechanics of it are mind-boggling.

tropes.name: Not So Above It All
tropes.html:
Jerry Springer gets into a fight with Dr Evil on his show.
Dr. Evil: "He's biting me! He's biting me!"

tropes.name: Offscreen Teleportation
tropes.html: When Dr. Evil and Mini-Me board the rocket to the moon, they are saluted by his minions who then somehow appear on the moon when they get there.

tropes.name: Once More, with Volume!
tropes.html:
Austin is giving a massage to Felicity who, upon being asked how it feels, requests Austin to move his hands further down along her back. Austin misinterprets and asks his same question but with a deeper voice.
Austin: [giving Felicity a massage] How does that feel, baby?
Felicity: Mmm, lower!
Austin: [deeper voice] How does that feel, baby?

tropes.name: OOC Is Serious Business
tropes.html: After Felicity dies, Austin chases Dr. Evil down with the intent to kill him. As in, not with the purpose of arresting a dangerous felon as within his duty as an international man of mystery, but hunting down Dr. Evil for the express purpose of murdering him. Dr. Evil only saves himself by mentioning that Austin could undo Felicity's death by using time travel.

tropes.name: Opening Narration
tropes.html: The late Tony Jay provides the narration for the film's Opening Scroll.

tropes.name: Papa Wolf
tropes.html: Dr. Evil gets in a fight with a KKK member for messing with Scott.

tropes.name: Parody Product Placement
tropes.html: Starbucks features quite heavily in the 90s-set portion of the movie... where it's revealed to be owned by Dr. Evil, courtesy of Number Two's prudent investing. Indeed, his new Supervillain Lair is a (fictional) Starbucks atop the Space Needle. Two even tries to persuade Evil to focus his business more on coffee than evil empires, on the grounds that they'll make a lot more money that way, but Evil is having none of it.

tropes.name: Perspective Reversal
tropes.html: In the first film, Austin upsets Vanessa by sleeping with Alotta as part of the job; in this movie, Felicity upsets Austin by sleeping with Fat Bastard as part of the job.

tropes.name: Pop-Cultural Osmosis Failure
tropes.html: Justified via Dr. Evil's frequent usage of references in his ransom video to the president; they were from media which doesn't even exist yet at the time. Funnily enough, this works in his favor when he "demonstrates" the laser's power by playing footage of the White House blowing up ripped straight from Independence Day, which initially scares everyone in the room into thinking that it was real.

tropes.name: Post-Climax Confrontation
tropes.html: Done with Fat Bastard but he gets defeated with a Groin Attack.

tropes.name: Prove I Am Not Bluffing
tropes.html: Dr. Evil blows up the White House to demonstrate his giant moon based laser... except it was just footage from Independence Day. Dr. Evil defends the real laser effect would be very similar.

tropes.name: Pun
tropes.html: Fat Bastard declares "I've got more chins than a Chinese phone book!" when lamenting about his weight.

tropes.name: Reflective Eyes
tropes.html: Austin sees an assassin about to throw a knife at him reflected in Robin's eyes.

tropes.name: Riddled and Rattled
tropes.html: Robin's body shakes wildly when Austin's uses her as a shield against a machine gun barrage.

tropes.name: Ridiculous Counter-Request
tropes.html:
When Ivana Humpalot says her name and Austin thinks she's making a request, he replies:
"Yeah, and I want a toilet made out of solid gold. It's just not in the cards now, is it?"

tropes.name: Robotic Reveal
tropes.html: When Austin rips off the Fembot's synthetic skin faceplate in the opening scene.

tropes.name: Sadistic Choice
tropes.html: Dr. Evil: Save the world... or save your girlfriend.

tropes.name: Sci-Fi Writers Have No Sense of Scale
tropes.html: When Dr.Evil threatens the President from his moon base, the General asks for permission to launch the U.S's nuclear arsenal to destroy the moon. In reality, the entire U.S nuclear arsenal going off at once would "only" make a crater about 10 km across, which wouldn't even be big enough to see with the naked eye from Earth, let alone destroy the entire thing.

tropes.name: Sequel Reset
tropes.html: "Wait a tick. That means I'm single again! Oh, behave!"

tropes.name: Sexy Surfacing Shot
tropes.html: In a parody of Honey Ryder's iconic scene in Dr. No, Felicity gracefully emerges on the beach in a white bikini...only to be followed by Austin doing the same, to both his and Felicity's confusion.

tropes.name: Shaking the Rump
tropes.html: When Felicity and Austin meet, Felicity turns and shakes her rear for him.

tropes.name: Shameless Fanservice Girl
tropes.html: Felicity. The majority of her outfits are skimpy and revealing (most likely part of her efforts to seduce Austin), and she has no problem flashing her panties while she and Austin tease a British Royal Guard, or showing her bare chest to an inept guard in order to lure him into her and Austin's cell.

tropes.name: Show Some Leg
tropes.html:
Felicity Shagwell bares her breasts to the one inept guard outside her and Austin's cell.
Felicity: What do you think of these, my man?
Guard: ...Mommy! (absentmindedly walks towards her and falls into the Lava Pit)

tropes.name: Sigil Spam
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's embossed logo can be found on nearly anything — makeup cases, motorized scooters, record turntables, even the doors of Dr. Evil's secret moon rocket.

tropes.name: "Signature Sport" Stereotype
tropes.html: Frau meets her lover Unibrau at an LPGA tournament.

tropes.name: Silence, You Fool!
tropes.html: "SILENCE! I will not tolerate your insolence!"

tropes.name: Smoking Hot Sex
tropes.html:
• Parodied at the beginning:
    Vanessa: Do you smoke after sex?
    Austin: I don't know, baby, I've never looked.
  • Felicity lights up after having sex with Fat Bastard.
  • Number Two and Number Two in a deleted scene—which, technically, isn't cheating.

tropes.name: Snake Versus Mongoose
tropes.html: Dr. Evil says, "Austin Powers... he's the snake to my mongoose, or the mongoose to my snake. Either way it's bad. I don't know animals."

tropes.name: Snap Back
tropes.html:
• Austin had cleaned up his teeth by the end of the first movie, but upon arriving back in 1969, he finds that they have reverted back to their original unhygenic state.
  • While lusting after Felicity, Austin "grooms" himself like a cat, which gets his hair all messed up. But by the time he and Felicity meet face to face, his hair is back to normal.

tropes.name: Something Something Leonard Bernstein
tropes.html: Dr. Evil and Mini Me attempt to perform "What If God Was One Of Us" for their assosciates. Dr Evil can only remember the lyrics to the first two lines and resorts to singing "bloo-bloo-bloo" to fill in the rest.

tropes.name: Space Base
tropes.html: Another one of Dr. Evil's supervillain lairs. He seems to have every variation of this trope covered.

tropes.name: Squirrels in My Pants
tropes.html: During Austin's fight with Mini-Me on the moonbase, Mini-Me rips a hole in the crotch part of Austin's space suit and proceeds to climb inside. Austin initially panics when Mini-Me begins to crawl around inside his suit, but then begins to fidget around and giggle saying that it tickles. He then traps Mini-Me and then proceeds to eject him out the rear end of his suit through a nearby space toilet.

tropes.name: Status Quo Is God
tropes.html: The previous movie ended with Austin marrying Vanessa Kensington. Here, Vanessa turns out to be a Fembot, rendering Austin single again.

tropes.name: Straight Gay
tropes.html: The Beefeater remains still when Felicity kisses him on one of his cheeks. When Austin does the same to the other cheek, the guard turns toward Austin and cheekily smiles.

tropes.name: Summon Backup Dancers
tropes.html: Felicity does this by pressing a button on Austin's wall. The flat is immediately swarmed by hippies ready for a party.

tropes.name: Surveillance Station Slacker
tropes.html: An operative at a NATO Surveillance facility switches one of the screens he's supposed to be monitoring to The Jerry Springer Show.

tropes.name: Sympathy for the Devil
tropes.html:
During their fight, Austin throws Mini-Me into a metal pole, and the clone drops to the floor, seemingly dead. Austin is quick to show regret over Mini-Me's "death".
Austin: He's so small. He's like a dog or something.

tropes.name: Talking Is a Free Action
tropes.html: When Austin travels back to save Felicity, he and his past self take a few moments to praise each other's handsomeness. This takes more time than it did for the poison gas to kill Felicity the first time around, yet she is clearly still alive throughout.

tropes.name: Talk Show Appearance
tropes.html: Dr. Evil and Scott go on Jerry Springer as a subject of dysfunctional fathers. Dr. Evil eventually incites a riot by getting into a fight with a Klansman and causes a riot.

tropes.name: Talk to the Hand
tropes.html:
Dr. Evil does this, much to the U.S. President of 1969's confusion, as Dr. Evil's using '90s-era pop culture lines... in 1969.
Dr. Evil: Talk to the hand, 'cause the face don't wanna hear it anymore.
The President: What hand? Talk to your hand?

tropes.name: The Tease
tropes.html: Felicity. As she makes her way over to Austin, she briefly dances with two other guys before pushing them away. She also kisses a British Royal Guard on the cheek in hopes of making him move.

tropes.name: Testes Test
tropes.html: After the Fembot blows up in his face at the beginning of the movie, Austin moves his hands to his crotch, then faces the camera and announces, "Oh, thank God."

tropes.name: Threat Backfire
tropes.html: In a deleted scene, Felicity responds to Austin telling her she's "going the right way for a smacked bottom" with a flirty "I hope so!"

tropes.name: Timey-Wimey Ball
tropes.html:
By virtue of time-travel.
Austin: Wait a tick. Basil, if I travel back to 1969 and I was frozen in 1967, presumably, I could go back and visit my frozen self. But, if I'm still frozen in 1967, how could I have been unthawed in the '90s and traveled back to— [goes cross-eyed in confusion] Oh, no, I've gone cross-eyed.
Basil: I suggest you don't worry about those things and just enjoy yourself. [to the camera] That goes for you all, too.

tropes.name: Trailer Spoof
tropes.html: Had one related to The Phantom Menace.

tropes.name: Trip to the Moon Plot
tropes.html: The movie's third act is about Dr. Evil installing a giant "laser" on the Moon and Austin following him there to stop him.

tropes.name: Unstoppable Rage
tropes.html: After a Klansmen called Scott Evil a "freak", Dr. Evil ends up going ballistic. He ends up fighting even when being restrained by Steve Wilkos and the other members of security, and after seemingly calming down, he then rushes to attack him again (something that never happens on the Jerry Springer show). And then instigates a full-out brawl on the set. Eventually, he seems calmed down... until Jerry Springer tells security to get Dr. Evil out of the premises ("get this jerk out of here"), upon which his rage is reawakened, and he starts fighting with the host, eventually managing to smash a globe in the ensuing stage riot.

tropes.name: Vader Breath
tropes.html: Mocked when Dr. Evil's spacesuit is damaged, giving him a deeper voice and interrupted breathing. Naturally, he takes this moment to tell Austin he is his father. (He isn't really.)

tropes.name: Villainous Valor
tropes.html: Despite being repeatedly used as a Bullet Proof Human Shield (and made to cushion Austin's fall), Robin scowls that Austin can't win.

tropes.name: Vocal Dissonance
tropes.html: At one point during the "Just The Two Of Us" musical number, the 2'8" Mini-Me sings a line in a very low baritone voice.

tropes.name: Voodoo Shark
tropes.html: Played for Laughs; Vanessa Kensington is revealed to be a Fembot, and apparently always was one... even though she was the daughter of Austin's old partner and we saw the two of them speaking as such in the first movie. Basil also apparently knew this the whole time and didn't say anything. Immediately after this revelation, the subject of Vanessa is dropped for the entire rest of the movie.

tropes.name: Wave-Motion Gun
tropes.html: The "Death Star" laser. (Ripoff!)

tropes.name: We Have Reserves
tropes.html:
When an accident with his chair results in Mini Me dangling from a pipe on the ceiling of the moon base, Dr. Evil invokes this trope.
Dr. Evil: Hang in there, Mini Me. If anything were to happen to you, I don't know what I would do. I'd probably move on and get another replica, but there would be a brief ten minute period where I would be just inconsolable.

tropes.name: White Flag
tropes.html: Austin waves one when under fire by the Fembot in the opening scene.

tropes.name: What Happened to the Mouse?
tropes.html: Austin's time-travelling VW Beetle is last seen in Austin's pad, with no mention of what happened to it later.

tropes.name: Why Won't You Die?
tropes.html: Austin asks this verbatim of Robin Swallows, who shrugs off a lot of lethal attacks.

tropes.name: Writers Cannot Do Math
tropes.html:
• Mini-Me is described as being "one-eighth" Dr. Evil's size. But he's clearly closer to a third of the doctor's size.
    • Actually this is roughly correct, it's just that 'size' is being used for volume/mass instead of height. Verne Troyer was just under half the height of Mike Myers, which would make his mass about an eighth.
  • Fat Bastard is said to weigh a "metric ton". For reference, that would be around 2000 lbs. He may be big, but he doesn't look anywhere near that big.
  • Austin is stated to have traveled back ten minutes in order to save Felicity, despite the fact that those events were closer to five minutes prior.

tropes.name: You Put the "X" in "XY"
tropes.html:
Invoked by Austin himself.
Robin Swallows: Tell me, Mr. Powers: Do you swing?
Austin: Are you kidding, baby? I put the "Grr" in "Swinger", baby!"

tropes.name: You Taste Delicious
tropes.html: During Austin and Felicity's Dance of Romance. Felicity licks Austin's cheek, following up with a kiss.

title: Planet of the Apes
intro: Adapted from the novel of the same name by French author Pierre Boulle, co-scripted by Rod Serling, and directed by Franklin J. Schaffner, this classic 1968 Science Fiction film launched a screen franchise that has continued, with various sequels, two television series, and reboots, into The New '20s. A team of astronauts flies into space at near-light speed. They are influenced by time dilation:

tropes.name: 20 Minutes into the Future
tropes.html: In the first scene, the year on the ship's onboard calendar reads 1972.

tropes.name: Adam and Eve Plot
tropes.html: Taylor mentions that Stewart, the only female astronaut, was to be their "Eve". Due to Time Dilation, the crew wasn't expected to return to Earth.

tropes.name: Adaptational Alternate Ending
tropes.html: In the original novel, the titular planet really is an alien planet called "Soror", which the main character and Nova escape by sneaking into an experimental space flight, only to discover that Earth has been also taken over by apes.

tropes.name: Adaptational Diversity
tropes.html: The four-astronaut crew in the film includes a black man and a woman. In the book, there were three white men and a chimp.

tropes.name: Adaptational Location Change
tropes.html: The film's planet turns out to be Earth All Along while the novel takes place on a different planet. The novel's protagonist eventually does return to Earth, but he lands in Paris instead of the New York / New Jersey area.

tropes.name: Adaptational Modesty
tropes.html:
• In the book, the wild humans walk around naked, as would be expected of their simian-like intellect. In the movie, they wear animal skins.
  • Likewise, when Ulysse (Taylor's counterpart) and his companions encounter the wild humans, they rip apart their clothes leaving them naked, while in the film they get their clothes stolen but find some ripped clothes to cover themselves.

tropes.name: Adaptation Name Change
tropes.html: Due to Adaptational Nationality change from an implied French crew to American, Ulysse Mérou is renamed George Taylor, Professor Antelle is Landon and Arthur Levain is Dodge.

tropes.name: Adaptational Species Change
tropes.html: Technical for the fourth companion of the spaceship who gets killed early on, along with a Gender Flip - in the book it is a pet chimp named Hector; in the film, a female astronaut named Stewart.

tropes.name: Adaptational Villainy
tropes.html: Unlike in the book, Dr. Zaius is aware that humans used to be the intelligent species on the planet and his plans to have Taylor vivisected or killed is part of the coverup. He also has Landon lobotomized for the same reason (in the book, Antelle just "degenerated" after being left in a cage with dumb humans) and later confesses to having killed other astronauts who arrived before Taylor.

tropes.name: After the End
tropes.html: The end reveals that Taylor didn't land on an alien planet but on Earth some two thousand years into the future, after the collapse of human civilization and its replacement by a simian one.

tropes.name: Agent Mulder
tropes.html: Zira is an unorthodox "animal psychologist" who thinks that humans can become intelligent and talk with adequate stimulation. Upon meeting Taylor, she takes his attempts to communicate as genuine and signs of greater intelligence in him, even though she still thinks of him as a gifted animal. That is until he reveals he can speak, which she accepts enthusiastically.

tropes.name: Agent Scully
tropes.html: Cornelius doubts Zira's theories even when presented with Taylor, though it is implied that this is encouraged by his desire to avoid conflict with Ape Law. When Taylor reveals he can speak, however, he immediately switches to treating him like an intelligent being, unlike Zaius or Julius.

tropes.name: Aliens Speaking English
tropes.html: The alien apes speak English and have Latin-inspired names, which go completely unremarked on by the visiting astronauts. However, this is subverted when it is revealed the planet was Earth All Along.

tropes.name: Alone in a Crowd
tropes.html: At the end of the film, Taylor and Nova set off into the Forbidden Zone and discover a large interesting-looking structure, only Taylor realises what it is note The Statue of Liberty and what has happened to humanity. Nova clearly has no clue what has happened or why Taylor is in despair.

tropes.name: Animal Is the New Man
tropes.html:
The astronauts land on a planet where apes are civilized and humans behave like animals. It is revealed in the end that the planet is Earth in the future.
Taylor: Man preceded you here. You owe him your science, your language, whatever knowledge you have.
Dr. Zaius: Then answer me this—if man was superior, why didn't he survive?

tropes.name: Anti-Hero
tropes.html: Taylor is a misanthropic, rather vicious Jerkass. However, he is not without sympathetic traits, such as his affection for Nova and his disgust with Landon's lobotomy. He also seems disappointed that the apes are no better than humans (or vice versa).

tropes.name: Anti-Villain
tropes.html: Doctor Zaius can be ruthless when pressed though he has fundamentally good intentions as he seeks to prevent humanity from causing another apocalypse and is at least reasonable enough to try and talk Taylor into making a false confession in exchange for his safety.

tropes.name: Apocalypse How
tropes.html: Taylor gets a Heroic BSoD when he learns that the planet is actually Earth after the collapse of civilization. Like the audiences of his time, he immediately assumes this was the result of nuclear war: "You maniacs! You blew it up!"

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Question
tropes.html:
• "Dr. Zaius, would an ape make a human doll that TALKS?"
  • "You do this out of fear. Because you're afraid of me! WHAT ARE YOU AFRAID OF, DOCTOR??"
  • Zaius himself gets one in the other direction: "If man was so superior, why didn't he survive?"

tropes.name: Artificial Gravity
tropes.html: In the opening scene, Taylor is seen walking over to his cryosleep pod to get inside while in outer space.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Biology
tropes.html:
• The ship is sent into space to colonize a new planet. That's why it contains three males and one female. A population that low would die out from inbreeding within several generations, even assuming the single female would reproduce constantly. For breeding, it would be far more efficient to have several females for each male, since a single male can impregnate multiple females, whereas a single female can only undergo one pregnancy at a time.
  • Gorillas are portrayed as warlike and violent, chimpanzees as reserved and rational, and orangutans as wise and social. Gorillas are very gentle and docile animals (though angering them is an extremely bad idea) while chimps have been known to exterminate other tribes, including the infants, to take the females and food. Orangutans have a completely anti-social society; males leave upon puberty and live on their own, attacking anyone who comes into their territory. However, some of this is a case of Science Marches On.
  • Every example of humans brawling with apes hand-to-hand underestimates what a Curb-Stomp Battle in the ape's favor would actually be. Even an adolescent chimp can toss a human around like a ragdoll if aggravated, and the larger apes could quite literally rip a human apart.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Linguistics
tropes.html: The Apes speak perfectly recognizable English more than two thousand years after Taylor left Earth.

tropes.name: Awful Truth
tropes.html: Dr. Zaius, and possibly the entire orangutan caste, knows the true history of the world and the origin of ape society.

tropes.name: Big Applesauce
tropes.html: Taylor finds the Statue of Liberty at the end of the film, revealing that the "Forbidden Zone" is where New York City used to be.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Doctor Zaius spends almost the entire film plotting against Taylor.

tropes.name: Black Dude Dies First
tropes.html: The only female astronaut dies due to a cryosleep malfunction while still on the ship, and the only black astronaut is killed during the first encounter with the apes, leaving only two white, male astronauts to see Ape City.

tropes.name: Bland-Name Product
tropes.html: The astronauts wear "ANSA" patches.

tropes.name: Captain's Log
tropes.html: Taylor makes an entry at the beginning of the film, before going into cryosleep.

tropes.name: Cassandra Truth
tropes.html: Plenty to pick up from: that Taylor is an intelligent being capable of speech, that humans once were intelligent and had a civilization, and that Taylor came from another planet in a spaceship. Even the apes who believe in Taylor in the first two cases don't in the third, and while the famous reveal proves them technically right, they are Right for the Wrong Reasons (they don't believe Taylor only because they don't believe powered flight is possible).

tropes.name: Characteristic Trope
tropes.html: This film made the Earth All Along trope its own, forcing later films to reference the film when featuring or referencing the trope in any form.

tropes.name: Chewing the Scenery
tropes.html: Charlton Heston all the way. You cut up his braaaaaaiiiinnn, you bloody baboon!; It's a madhouse! A MAAADHOUSE!!! (Lampshaded in the trailer), his very weird braying and over-the-top grin of HAW HAW HAW HAW, and especially YOU MANIACS! YOU BLEW IT UP! OH, DAMN YOU! GOD DAMN YOU ALL TO HELL! — are just a few times he does it during the movie.

tropes.name: Color-Coded Castes
tropes.html: Chimpanzees wear green, gorillas wear black/purple, and orangutans wear orange.

tropes.name: Comic Trio
tropes.html: The apes' society is based on this. The orangutans run things, the gorillas carry their plans out, and the chimpanzees have all the brains and none of the power.

tropes.name: Composite Character
tropes.html: Taylor is actually a mix between the protagonist Ulysse, who tries to prove to Zira that he's intelligent, and the misanthropic professor Antelle who's tired of humans in the book.

tropes.name: The Constant
tropes.html: Taylor finally realizes that he's actually on future Earth and not on another planet when he finds the remains of the Statue of Liberty half buried in the sand.

tropes.name: Cryonics Failure
tropes.html: Happens before the spaceship crashes in the titular planet. For the men, it just means they wake up with longer hair and full beards, but the only woman Stewart ages into an 80+-looking woman and dies without waking up.

tropes.name: Crystal Dragon Jesus
tropes.html: The ape religion is definitely Abrahamaic; they outright have "God", who made apes in his image and condemned humans. References to The Lawgiver as the writer of the Sacred Scrolls that serve as the basis for the Ape religion, with no apparent divine nature of his own, put their religion closer to Judaism or Islam than Christianity.

tropes.name: Cute Mute
tropes.html: Nova, a beautiful woman who cannot speak, becomes Taylor's love interest. In his (somewhat sleazy) words, she's "not much for conversation" but she's "the only girl in town".

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html: Taylor, even when mute. Cornelius fits the bill among the apes.

tropes.name: Dead Guy on Display
tropes.html: After being killed on the hunt, Dodge's body is stuffed and placed in the human exhibit of a museum. A tie-in comic added further context by claiming that the apes did this because they had never seen a dark-skinned man before.

tropes.name: Despair Event Horizon
tropes.html: The revelation that it was Earth All Along drop-kicks Taylor right across it. He spends his final seconds on screen crying and screaming insults at those who made the end of the world happen.

tropes.name: Detonation Moon
tropes.html: Implied to have happened since we're on Earth, but Taylor and his fellow astronauts note that the sky has no moon.

tropes.name: Developing Doomed Characters
tropes.html: It's at least a half hour until we encounter the apes, and all but one of the astronauts either ends up dead or lobotomized.

tropes.name: Does This Remind You of Anything?
tropes.html: At his hearing, Taylor is repeatedly reminded that as a human, he has no rights under ape law - mirroring the ruling of Dredd Scott's trial, which stated that African-Americans were not citizens of the US regardless if they were slave or free.

tropes.name: Downer Ending
tropes.html:
After Zira and Cornelius get hauled away to be tried for heresy, it is revealed that the planet of the apes was Earth All Along, thousands of years after World War III. Taylor was home all along, and the home he was hoping to get back to was gone. His final howl of despair implies the realization has completely broken him.
Taylor: We finally, really did it...YOU MANIACS! YOU BLEW IT UP! Ah, damn you! God damn you all to hell!

tropes.name: Dub Name Change
tropes.html: Of all the characters, Cornelius alone got his name changed for the Spanish dub. He was renamed "Aurelio." This change is particularly mystifying, because "Cornelius" (being a name of Latin origin) does have a Spanish form: "Cornelio".

tropes.name: Earth All Along
tropes.html: The Trope Codifier. The "planet of the apes" is Earth, thousands of years after a nuclear holocaust.

tropes.name: Eerily Out-of-Place Object
tropes.html: The Statue of Liberty on a beach on what was supposed to be an alien planet.

tropes.name: Eiffel Tower Effect
tropes.html: Seeing the Statue of Liberty allows Taylor to realize that he's actually on Earth.

tropes.name: Empathy Doll Shot
tropes.html: Used as a plot point. The apes in an archeological site are freaked out when a human doll talks.

tropes.name: Escaped Animal Rampage
tropes.html: A funny inversion occurs when Taylor, the human, escapes from a medical lab where apes do experiments on humans. He then runs amok, scaring the innocent residents of Ape City.

tropes.name: Eternal English
tropes.html: It's over two thousand years in the future, and the apes speak perfect English. Although they don't call it that... Cornelius just says it was the language taught to him by his father and his father before him.

tropes.name: Evil Laugh
tropes.html: Not really "evil" so much as mockingly cynical, but Taylor's laughter at Landon planting a tiny U.S. flag on the planet has a similar effect.

tropes.name: Evolutionary Levels
tropes.html: The apes' evolution to intelligence, and humanity's loss of it in a couple of thousand years.

tropes.name: Fantastic Caste System
