tropes.html: Gorillas are soldiers, police, and blue-collar workers. Chimpanzees work in the medical and academic fields. Orangutans are the lawmaking aristocracy. It's mentioned that the caste system was abolished, but that only pertains to it being officially institutionalized. In practice, it's still very much in effect.

tropes.name: Fantastic Racism
tropes.html:
Apes hate humans. And their society is clearly divided between chimps, gorillas, and orangutans. It's even said that during production the cast would spontaneously segregate by the ape costumes they wore.
Honorius: Why are all apes created equal?
Taylor: Some apes, it seems, are more equal than others.
Honorius: Ridiculous! That answer is a contradiction in terms.

tropes.name: Fate Worse than Death
tropes.html:
• Dodge's body is stuffed and put on display at a museum, likely with nobody ever knowing he was an intelligent man.
  • Landon is captured alive but later ends up lobotomized, implicitly on orders of Dr. Zaius to keep the existence of intelligent humans secret. He is last seen being whipped to make him get in a cage with other primitive humans.
  • Taylor himself becomes more desperate to escape after learning that he is scheduled to be lobotomized himself, and also emasculated, and also going to lose his two best friends to a Kangaroo Court on heresy charges.

tropes.name: Forbidden Zone
tropes.html: A lifeless desert not far from Ape City, literally called "The Forbidden Zone", is closed off to ape citizens by their government because it holds evidence that humans once were the dominant species over the planet.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: When Zaius spots Taylor’s writing in the dirt, rather than expressing astonishment or confusion, he simply wipes away it with his walking stick before anyone else can see it, an early hint that he knows more about man’s capacity for intelligence than he’s letting on.

tropes.name: For Science!
tropes.html: Landon says that Dodge would walk naked into a live volcano if it meant he could learn something that no one else knew.

tropes.name: Freudian Threat
tropes.html: Dr. Zaius makes repeated attempts to emasculate Taylor, potentially due to his obsession with the idea of a race of intelligent humans breeding.

tropes.name: Getting Crap Past the Radar
tropes.html: There were concerns that censors would object to Taylor's cry of "God damn you all to hell!" under Section V of the Hays Code. The problem was avoided when the producers and Heston explained that the phrase was not an expletive. Rather, Taylor was, literally, calling on God to damn the entire human race for destroying civilization.

tropes.name: Gone Swimming, Clothes Stolen
tropes.html: The astronauts' immediate reaction to discovering a (freshwater) lake just outside of the Forbidden Zone is to go Skinny Dipping. While this happens, their clothes and equipment end up being stolen and destroyed by the primitive humans.

tropes.name: Ham-to-Ham Combat
tropes.html: Charlton Heston and Maurice Evans spend much of the movie's final third trying to out-act one another, as Taylor and Dr. Zaius verbally spar over and over. The fact that Heston more than keeps up with Evans despite Evans having the advantage of being costumed as an orangutan speaks to his Large Ham mastery.

tropes.name: Hero of Another Story
tropes.html: An Ape organization called the Anti-Vivisection League is mentioned a few times as a rare group that fights for human rights and tries to prevent people like Zaius from sterilizing human slaves. No known members appear onscreen, though.

tropes.name: History Repeats
tropes.html: After humanity blew itself up with nuclear weapons, their descendants regressed into primitive creatures comparable to Australopithecines. Meanwhile, the Apes repeated the same history of segregation, oppression, and violence as the humans they despise so much.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: Taylor wins his freedom and rides off with Nova to find his place on the Planet of the Apes... only to learn that it is Earth All Along.

tropes.name: Hope Sprouts Eternal
tropes.html: At first it appears that the planet is completely desolate, but they look for signs of life anyway. They discover that it has life when they see a small dandelion plant growing in the desert. "Where there's one, there must be more!" So, hope renewed, they keep looking.

tropes.name: Human Aliens
tropes.html: The apes and the humans look exactly like the ones on Earth. Subverted Trope when it turns out it was Earth All Along.

tropes.name: Humans Are Bastards
tropes.html:
Eloquently declared in The Sacred Scrolls.
"Beware the beast, Man, for he is the Devil’s pawn. Alone among God’s primates, he kills for sport. Or lust. Or greed. Yea, he will murder his brother to possess his brother’s land. Let him not breed in great numbers, for he will make a desert of his home and yours. Shun him. Drive him back into his jungle lair, for he is the harbinger of death."

tropes.name: Humans Are Morons
tropes.html: Subverted. Humans degenerated after blowing themselves up in a nuclear war, but there is no sign that the apes that replaced them are any better, they might just be walking in the human race's footsteps to a similar fate, despite considering themselves oh-so superior.

tropes.name: Humans Are the Real Monsters
tropes.html: Taylor feels this way at the beginning, but after meeting the apes, he changes his mind. Then comes the ending, which is when it's all but confirmed. Downplayed Trope, as what we see of the Apes suggests that they have all the same flaws that the humans had and it's only their primitive technology that keeps them from doing as much damage.

tropes.name: Humans Are Ugly
tropes.html: When Taylor wants to kiss Zira goodbye, she consents but not without adding that he is "so damned ugly."

tropes.name: Human Popsicle
tropes.html: The astronauts originate in the remote past compared to the events in most of the film, due to traveling in a Sleeper Starship.

tropes.name: Idiot Ball
tropes.html: The decision to go skinny dipping directly leads to two of the three astronauts dying as they end up losing their only gun. What pushes this decision into idiocy territory as opposed to just negligence on their part is that Taylor dismisses the scarecrows as he called them on the approach to the lake which could have just as easily been warning signs marking territory. They knew that they were not alone and yet they completely disarmed themselves anyway.

tropes.name: In Name Only
tropes.html: When compared to the original novel, which was set on a different planet, and gave the apes 20th-century tech, the main character was accepted into ape society until he had a son, and they even allowed him to return to Earth (briefly).

tropes.name: ...In That Order
tropes.html: "If they catch you, they will dissect you. And kill you. In that order."

tropes.name: In Your Nature to Destroy Yourselves
tropes.html: Dr. Zaius explains to Taylor that his bigotry against humans is because they ultimately destroy any environment they settle in. Towards the end, Dr. Cornelius (who is actually sympathetic to Taylor) even reads from a religious scroll that warns of "that harbinger of Death — man". The ending reveals that Zaius was completely right since it's really a post-apocalyptic future.

tropes.name: Irony
tropes.html:
• In the prologue, Taylor wonders if there's a sentient race out there that's "better than man." It turns out most of the Apes are hardly any better than the humans they claim to be superior to. For further irony, this might have been prevented had the Apes' leaders been honest about the history of humanity and the world so that all Apes could learn from humanity's mistakes, rather than covering it up to pretend like humans were always unintelligent beasts and Apes were always the superior, dominant species.
  • He also starts off as a cynical misanthrope who couldn't wait to get away from the human race. By the halfway point of the movie, he's forced to become humanity's vocal proponent. And then the ending reveals he was right about humans being bastards all along.
  • There's also a distinctly harsh moment where Taylor is roughly tying up Doctor Zaius near the finale, despite the protests of Zira and Cornelius; Taylor blithely remarks that it's no different from how he was treated, suggesting that he's no better than the Apes.

tropes.name: Insult Backfire
tropes.html:
Taylor: Dr. Zaius, I know who I am but who are you? How in hell did this upside-down civilization get started?
Zaius: Huh! You may well call it upside-down since you occupy its lowest level, and deservedly so.

tropes.name: Ironic Name
tropes.html: Dodge is fatally shot by the apes (twice, technically), never dodging any bullets.

tropes.name: Is This a Joke?
tropes.html: The tribunal dismisses Taylor's claim of being from another planet as "a joke."

tropes.name: I Want My Jet Pack
tropes.html: 1972 has come and gone, and while we stepped foot on the Moon the year after this movie's release, we do not have spaceships with Artificial Gravity, hypersleep chambers, and engines that can (at least theoretically) allow the ship to travel 300 light-years at near the speed of light.

tropes.name: Jerkass
tropes.html: Most of Taylor's behavior toward the apes for most of the film. He doesn't appear to get along particularly well with his fellow astronauts, either.

tropes.name: Jerkass Has a Point
tropes.html: Dr. Zaius at the very end, although the point is not made by him.

tropes.name: Kangaroo Court
tropes.html: Taylor is subjected to a "hearing" with all the appearance of a trial, except the very apes judging him do not accuse him of anything in particular and point out several times that as a man, he has no rights under ape law. Cornelius and Zira are later threatened with being subjected to another Kangaroo Court on charges of heresy for having been Taylor's advocates, even though they are apes and have those theoretical rights.

tropes.name: Killer Space Monkey
tropes.html: The gorilla hunters that the astronauts encounter soon after jumping out of their spaceship fit the trope, even if they are revealed to have never left Earth in the end.

tropes.name: Land of One City
tropes.html: Ape City doesn't appear to control other settlements despite having ministries and such.

tropes.name: Large Ham
tropes.html:
• Charlton Heston as Taylor is a strong candidate for the hammiest lead performance in Hollywood history.
    "It's a MAAAAAAADHOOOOUSE!!! A MAAAAAAADHOOOOOOOUUUUUUUUSE!!!!!!!!"
  • Maurice Evans as Dr. Zaius has his moments too.
    "The Forbidden Zone was once a paradise! Your breed made a desert of it!"

tropes.name: Laser-Guided Karma
tropes.html: At the end of the film, after being repeatedly attacked, beaten, caged, stripped, and tied up by the apes, Taylor exacts a small measure of revenge by capturing Dr. Zaius, arguably the Apes' main spokesperson, and tying him to a log.

tropes.name: Last-Name Basis
tropes.html: All astronauts are referred to by their last names, with even Taylor's only becoming known in the sequel.

tropes.name: Lobotomy
tropes.html: Landon is lobotomized by the apes, implicitly on orders of Dr. Zaius to keep the existence of intelligent humans a secret.

tropes.name: Low Culture, High Tech
tropes.html: The apes wield repeating rifles (the movie props are modified M1 carbines), at least a century more advanced than any other tech they're shown using.

tropes.name: Monkey Morality Pose
tropes.html: The orangutan judges adopt the pose during Taylor's hearing, fitting the first two's refusal to hear and see the truth (that Taylor is an intelligent being) while Dr. Zaius knows the truth but refuses to speak it.

tropes.name: Monumental Damage
tropes.html: Near the 40th century, the Statue of Liberty — though half-buried and severely damaged — is the only part of New York City still recognizable.

tropes.name: Morally Ambiguous Doctorate
tropes.html: Dr. Zaius: Ethically questionable... OK, very unethical. In fact, an antagonist. He routinely performs lethal experiments on those inferior humans, although he later explains why he's so wary of man.

tropes.name: Motherly Scientist
tropes.html: Dr. Zira, a notable psychologist and zoologist, calls Taylor "Bright Eyes," at least until he manages to write his own name, to her surprise. She ends up kissing him goodbye - even though, as she tells him, "You're so damned ugly." She's sort of like a reverse Jane Goodall.

tropes.name: Mr. Fanservice
tropes.html: Taylor, who provides perhaps the most male nudity you'll ever find in a G-rated film. He goes Skinny Dipping along with the other astronauts during the above-mentioned Gone Swimming, Clothes Stolen scene, and his state of dress doesn't really change from there on out. We also get to see his naked ass on at least two separate occasions.

tropes.name: Not So Above It All
tropes.html: The ape society as a whole. For as much as they like to look down on humans, the fact that the apes hunt non-sapient humans for sport, have political corruption and religious fanaticism shows that the apes are hypocritical (albeit mostly unknowingly) and likely to follow in humanity’s self-destructive footsteps.

tropes.name: Nubile Savage
tropes.html: Nova, who spends most of her time scantily-clad.

tropes.name: OOC Is Serious Business
tropes.html: The apes are only familiar with unintelligent, non-speaking humans. So when Taylor starts writing, it scares Cornelius and Zira before it impresses them. Everyone is scared when his throat wound heals and he's able to say his iconic line: "Take your stinking paws off me, you damned dirty ape."

tropes.name: Outside-Context Problem
tropes.html: Despite being captive, enslaved, and thought to be mute, Taylor is out of context to the apes once they realize that he can write, is quite intelligent, and eventually talks once his throat is healed. All the other humans in the film are kept as pets who can't talk or think intelligently.

tropes.name: Persecution Flip
tropes.html: The apes hunt and mutilate humans, keep them in cages, and use them for experiments, and think they don't deserve any better than that.

tropes.name: Pet the Dog
tropes.html:
• Dr. Zaius's final warning to Taylor when he sets off to find out more about the planet. He even calls Taylor by his name, acknowledging him as his equal.
Taylor: A planet where apes evolved from men? There's got to be an answer.
Dr. Zaius: Don't look for it, Taylor. You may not like what you find.
  • The leader of the hunting party that guns down dozens of humans and roughly drags many more around in nets is relatively gentle with the one human child the group takes prisoner.
  • President Gaius is by no means a Reasonable Authority Figure, but he does at least make an attempt to rein in the state's prosecutor Dr Honorius when he goes off on a slanderous tangent aimed at Cornelius and Zira.

tropes.name: Post-Historical Trauma
tropes.html: Taylor learns about World War III two millennia later and falls into despair, yelling "You maniacs! You blew it up! Damn you!! GOD DAMN YOU ALL TO HELL!!!"

tropes.name: Pragmatic Adaptation
tropes.html:
• In the original novel, the apes live in a society that is identical to the 1960's, when the book was written. Due to budgetary reasons, their city is more primitive with the most advanced things they have been automatic guns, pens, and hoses.
  • The titular planet is indeed a different planet in the novel, which is guilty of Casual Interplanetary Travel. After his adventure, Nova and Ulysse (Taylor) return to Earth, only to find that it has been taken over by apes in his absence. The movie condenses both by making it Earth All Along.
  • While the archaeological site and the doll are both present in the novel, Dr. Zaius is not aware of man's past preeminence, and this is discovered only when Nova is subjected to an experiment that unlocks her ancestor's Genetic Memory.
  • The movie also eliminates yet another final twist that reveals the story was a message in a bottle found "adrift" in space by two scientists, who turn out to be apes, probably from yet another planet, who also think that the idea of intelligent humans is ridiculous.

tropes.name: Precision F-Strike
tropes.html:
• "GOD DAMN YOU ALL TO HELL!!!"
  • "Take your stinking paws off me, you damn dirty ape!"

tropes.name: Punctuated!  For!  Emphasis!
tropes.html: Delivered as only Charlton Heston can say it. All together now: GOD! DAMN! YOU! ALL! TO! HELL!

tropes.name: Real Life Writes the Plot
tropes.html: The ape society was originally going to be more technologically advanced, akin to the book it was based on, but it proved too expensive and the ape society was made more primitive to cut costs.

tropes.name: Sacred Scripture
tropes.html: The Sacred Scrolls, written by The Lawgiver, are the basis of the ape religion.

tropes.name: Scary Scarecrows
tropes.html: Just before leaving the Forbidden Zone, the three surviving astronauts find scarecrows with the appearance of corpses tied to a St. Andrew's cross.

tropes.name: Schizo Tech
tropes.html: The apes use modified M1 carbines and photo cameras, but don't think airplanes are possible (never mind interplanetary travel) and use horses and carts instead of motor-powered vehicles. It is possible that some technologies are being delayed by Dr. Zaius and the orangutans just like the knowledge of human civilization, but it is never confirmed.

tropes.name: Secret Police
tropes.html: Dr. Zaius knows that ape society's view of humanity is not entirely true, and because of what he knows, he's deeply involved in making sure that that stays true, prosecuting Taylor's collaborators for heresy rather than letting out the fact that humans are actually sentient beings.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: To Animal Farm. When asked if he knows why all apes were created equal, Taylor replies that "some apes seem to be more equal than others". The prosecutor's response is, "Ridiculous! A contradiction in terms."

tropes.name: Silent Credits
tropes.html: One of the most famous silent end credits (except for the sound of waves crashing on the shore) as Taylor realizes he's been on Earth all along.

tropes.name: Sleeper Starship
tropes.html: The crew hibernates during the trip, but Cryonics Failure leads to them aging normally before waking up.

tropes.name: Spoiler Cover
tropes.html: Videotape covers were showing the Statue of Liberty on the cover, spoiling the Twist Ending.

tropes.name: Status Quo Is God
tropes.html: At the beginning of the film, Taylor believes humanity to be bastards, but changes his mind after meeting the apes, but goes right back to thinking it after seeing the ruins of the Statue of Liberty. In the sequel, becomes even more misanthropic.

tropes.name: The Theocracy
tropes.html: Ape society runs pretty heavily on laws created by the ape version of Moses, and is intolerant of acts of heresy. It's also implied that the ruling caste is deliberately holding back scientific progress to prevent society from changing.

tropes.name: Time Dilation
tropes.html: Taylor's crew ages 18 months while 2006 years have passed outside.

tropes.name: Time-Passage Beard
tropes.html: The first telling evidence of the Cryonics Failure that the astronauts get is noticing that they have grown beards.

tropes.name: Tomato Surprise
tropes.html: Taylor finds the ruined Statue of Liberty and realizes he was on Earth All Along.

tropes.name: Twist Ending
tropes.html: The Planet of the Apes was Earth All Along. Considering Rod Serling had a hand in the 1968 screenplay, it really shouldn't have been that surprising.

tropes.name: Well-Intentioned Extremist
tropes.html:
Dr. Zaius, to an extent. In any case, he obviously already knows what Taylor would discover in the ending.
Dr. Zaius: All my life I've awaited your coming and dreaded it. Like death itself.
Taylor: Why? I've terrified you from the first, Doctor. I still do. You're afraid of me and you hate me. Why?
Dr. Zaius: Because you're a man! And you're right, I have always known about man. From the evidence, I believe his wisdom must walk hand in hand with his idiocy. His emotions must rule his brain. He must be a warlike creature who gives battle to everything around him, even himself.
Taylor: What evidence? There were no weapons in that cave.
Dr. Zaius: The Forbidden Zone was once a paradise. Your breed made a desert of it, ages ago.
Taylor: That still doesn't give me the why. A planet where apes evolved from men? There's got to be an answer.
Dr. Zaius: Don't look for it, Taylor. You may not like what you find.

tropes.name: Wham Line
tropes.html:
The first words the apes hear from a human, ever, is none other than "TAKE YOUR STINKING PAWS OFF OF ME, YOU DAMNED DIRTY APE!!!" Made all the more powerful if you know that Charlton Heston was sick with the flu at the time, but the director felt that the hoarseness of his voice would add impact to that line. It did.
  • Additionally, Taylor at the archaeological dig when Nova, holding the doll, accidentally triggers its voicebox, undermining Dr. Zaius' and ape society's claim that man has always been a brute animal:
    Taylor: Dr. Zaius, would an ape make a human doll...that talks?

tropes.name: Wham Shot
tropes.html: The Statue of Liberty at the end. For people who didn't know beforehand, at least.

tropes.name: You Called Me "X"; It Must Be Serious
tropes.html: Publicly, Dr. Zaius insists that Taylor must be an animal trained in mimicry or some other fraud, and insists on calling him by Zira's original nickname for him, Bright Eyes. When meeting privately with Taylor to negotiate, however, Zaius dispenses with all such political double talk, talking to Taylor as a fellow intelligent being, and calling him by his real name. Taylor even thanks him for it.

tropes.name: You Can Talk?
tropes.html: When Taylor says the Wham Line above, all the apes go dead silent. They don't say this quote word for word, but their expressions sure do.

title: Taken 2
intro: Taken 2 is a 2012 French action thriller film starring Liam Neeson, produced and written by Luc Besson and directed by Pierre Morel, and the sequels by Olivier Megaton. It is a sequel to Taken (2008). The stage is moved to İstanbul, with the families of the first movie's band of sex slave traders seeking revenge by kidnapping Bryan Mills (Neeson) and Lenore (Famke Janssen) while they are on a vaca

tropes.name: Action Film, Quiet Drama Scene
tropes.html: Right after an intense car chase in Istanbul and crashing through a checkpoint to get to the US Embassy, Bryan and Kim share a moment in the car (in which they are waiting for Bryan's friend Sam to call someone else up at the embassy to make sure they don't get shot at) where Kim asks what happened to Lenore, to which Bryan replies that Lenore wasn't able to, though she is still alive and is likely to be tortured for information. Bryan then reassures Kim that he's going to find the people that are after them and make sure they don't bother him or anybody else in their family for the rest of their lives.

tropes.name: All There in the Script
tropes.html: Suko's name is only stated in the film's casting credits.

tropes.name: Always Chaotic Evil
tropes.html: The Albanians again. Their reasons for vengeance earn them no sympathy points.

tropes.name: Amicably Divorced
tropes.html: Continuing the trend from the end of the first movie, Bryan and Lenore have this dynamic. Predictably, they get a Relationship Upgrade. Based on trailers, you would've been forgiven for thinking that it had already happened.

tropes.name: And Your Little Dog, Too!
tropes.html:
• When the Albanians torture Jean-Claude, they show him his child's plush toy.
  • Murad tells Bryan that they will find his daughter and sell her all over again, this time to the lowest bidder to be defiled until she is nothing but a piece of meat.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html:
At one point, Bryan and Kim together triangulate his position over cellphone by having her set off a loud noise (in this case a grenade) and him counting how long it takes him to hear it through his phone versus through the air. The problem is, cell phone conversations are rarely instantaneous; there's typically a portion-of-a-second lag between transmission and reception. While it would be in-character for Bryan to be able to factor this into his calculations, such reasoning could easily lead to Fan Wank, so let us simply say that this issue was not addressed.
  • For that matter, Bryan's calculations aren't even accurate. He counts off 4.5 seconds between Kim detonating a grenade to when he hears it, and so concludes that he is at a 4.5 miles radius from Kim, a 1 second to 1 mile ratio. However, the speed of sound in air is ~340 mps, so the correct calculation of Bryan's distance from Kim should have an approximate radius of 1.6 km, or just under one mile.
  • It was a rough estimate. He didn't need down-to-the-meter precision, just a general sense - that is to say, "Are you one mile away? Two? Ten?". Once he gets a rough estimate of distance, he realistically uses local landmarks to get an exact fix.

tropes.name: Avenging the Villains
tropes.html: The film's premise is the families of the Albanian kidnappers from the first movie attempting to get revenge on Bryan for killing them.

tropes.name: Backseat Driver
tropes.html: Bryan guides Kim to the U.S. embassy in a "borrowed" cab. Given that it's someone without a license and an action movie, much havoc is unleashed on Istanbul's streets.

tropes.name: Badass Longcoat
tropes.html: Whenever he goes outside while on the way to capture or check on someone, Murad is seen wearing a black trenchcoat.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Murad Hoxha, the leader of the Albanians seeking revenge on Bryan for killing their relatives in the first film. Specifically, Murad is the father of Marko Hoxha, one of the first film's two Big Bads.

tropes.name: Bottomless Magazines
tropes.html:
• Especially during the car chase, Bryan fires his automatic pistol far more times than the magazine would allow and is never shown reloading.
  • Averted later when Bryan gets his hands on an AK-47. He squeezes the trigger once for a few seconds into the gut of a mook before dropping the gun, the magazine spent. Also averted in the scene where mooks fire automatic weapons, as they need to reload the guns several times.

tropes.name: The Brute
tropes.html: One of the most prominent Albanians aside from Murad is a big guy named Suko, who does much of the physical work, including torturing both Jean-Claude and Bryan. He takes Lenore with him at Murad's order and proves to be nearly Bryan's match later in the climax.

tropes.name: Bullying a Dragon
tropes.html:
The bad guys know for a fact that Bryan, on his own, cut his way through their sex slavery ring like a hot knife through butter leaving a trail of bodies behind him that would make a serial killer blush. This is the man they intentionally want to antagonize. Vengeance is one thing, but this borders on suicidal recklessness.
  • They started it because they were hurt at their loss after having lost several people from the village. They lost a lot more people than that in their foolish revenge scheme.

tropes.name: But for Me, It Was Tuesday
tropes.html:
Murad shows Bryan photographs of the men he killed in the previous film. The only one he can remember is Murad's son, the one he tortured to death by electrocuting him through nails in his legs.
Murad: You recognize none of them. To you, they were nothing, but to other people, they are... sons and grandsons, fathers and husbands. And you killed them all, like they were so many nothings. (shows Bryan a photo of Marko) And this one? You recognize him? You do recognize him. Him, you didn't just kill; him, you strapped to a chair, you attached electric cables to the chair, you turned the current on, and you left it on... until his heart burst.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html:
• When Lenore tells Bryan not to go looking into Jamie, he tries to protest that he doesn't even know his name. She reminds him that he found Kim in a city of 12 million people in less than 72 hours.
  • Bryan and his buddies still get together for red meat and red wine.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gag
tropes.html: At the beginning of the film, Kim is having a difficult time passing her driver's test. During the epilogue, there is a closeup of a distressed Bryan, which is meant to suggest he or his family is in peril again. Then the film cuts to a wide angle shot to discover he's just watching Kim parallel park for her driver's test.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Skill
tropes.html: Kim learning how to drive.

tropes.name: Choke Holds
tropes.html: Bryan puts a twist on this technique by using a pistol to choke an elderly Albanian against a wall

tropes.name: The Coats Are Off
tropes.html: Bryan at the end.

tropes.name: Concealment Equals Cover
tropes.html: Averted when Bryan is shot at through a wall.

tropes.name: Crazy-Prepared
tropes.html: It comes as part of Bryan's job as a bodyguard to always have the necessary equipment needed to make sure that he can get out of any situation, but this film is where it's really shown. For the trip to Istanbul, he brings himself a suitcase full of recording equipment, cash and passports accessible at a moment's notice, plus a hidden cell phone and even a couple hand grenades just in case. These preparations prove handy when Kim tells him that strange men have entered the hotel she's in.

tropes.name: Cycle of Revenge
tropes.html: Discussed in the final confrontation between Bryan and Murad. Murad tells Bryan that if he kills him, then his other two sons will seek revenge too, to which Bryan ensures him that they'll die the same way. Bryan mentions, however, that Murad can instead go home and spend time with his sons and grandchildren; his killing of Marko is merely the price of being in a criminal business like human trafficking, and echoes the loss of all the lives Marko ruined.

tropes.name: Delayed Reaction
tropes.html: At the living room where several Albanians are watching soccer on TV, the Albanian who decides to exit takes a while to properly react to Bryan suddenly appearing with a gun at his face, only walking back while dropping his things, then screaming just before Bryan shoots him dead and the other Albanians realize they're in danger right at that moment.

tropes.name: Disney Villain Death
tropes.html: In the climax, Bryan takes advantage of the multi-floor balconies around him by dropping Mooks from them, whether it be by shooting them down or throwing them off.

tropes.name: The Don
tropes.html: Murad.

tropes.name: Dramatic Gun Cock
tropes.html: Bryan's cue to duck before two mooks unleash a hail of assault rifle fire through the wall at him.

tropes.name: Drives Like Crazy
tropes.html: Subverted while playing it straight. Kim has failed her driver's license test twice now, yet she can drive perfectly when Bryan is giving her instructions. Guess who has to drive wildly through the streets of Istanbul while avoiding the police, and who's giving them the orders?

tropes.name: Driving Stick
tropes.html: Guess what kind of car is used in the aforementioned chase.

tropes.name: Due to the Dead
tropes.html: After defeating Suko, The Brute of the Albanians, Bryan appears to close his eyes in respect for the toughest fight of his life, though it's not visually clear.

tropes.name: Empathy Doll Shot
tropes.html: In their interrogation on Jean-Claude, one of the Albanians shows him his son's teddy bear to clarify that they're willing to kill not only him but also his family (although it's ambiguous whether they already did the latter or are threatening that they'll do it) if he doesn't give them any information about Bryan's whereabouts.

tropes.name: Even Evil Has Loved Ones
tropes.html: Uh oh, Bryan, did we mention that the kidnappers you killed have families and friends in Albania, and they're VERY angry with you now?

tropes.name: Evil Counterpart
tropes.html: Murad comes off as something of an evil Bryan with his Papa Wolf characterization, as well as sporting a similar Badass Longcoat once.

tropes.name: Facepalm of Doom
tropes.html: Bryan kills Murad this way, pushing his head on to a towel hook, impaling his head with it.

tropes.name: Famous-Named Foreigner
tropes.html:
So, can we conclude that Murad Hoxha is related to the late communist ruler of Albania?
  • Hoxha originally was a Turkish title (Hoca).

tropes.name: Faux Affably Evil
tropes.html: Murad. There's a trope-defining scene where Lenore is talking to him, and Murad mentions how he admires her, how he thinks she's a innocent woman who had nothing to do with his son's death, and then he says for such respect he'll send her back home... in pieces.

tropes.name: Flashback
tropes.html: There are plenty of them made by reusing footage from the first movie. Later, there's also a few from earlier scenes in the film itself.

tropes.name: Foregone Conclusion
tropes.html: At the end, Murad says that he has two sons that will avenge him if he dies at Bryan's hands. Without batting an eye, Bryan says he'll just kill them too if that's the case. And sure enough, they're not in the third movie, although whether it was because of that or something else is unknown.

tropes.name: Fruit Cart
tropes.html: A few of them get smashed during the sequence where Bryan tries to get away from the Albanians going after him on car. Not just fruit carts either; bagels and a few other carts.

tropes.name: Genre Blindness
tropes.html: Despite having a pretty good idea of what Bryan is capable of, Murad still insists on prolonging his suffering and explaining what he intends to do to Bryan's family, then proceeds to not have a few dozen mooks with guns trained on him at all times. This turns out to be exactly as bad a plan as it sounds.

tropes.name: Gilligan Cut
tropes.html: The scene with the background check joke segues directly into Bryan arriving at the house of Kim's boyfriend Jamie.

tropes.name: Googling the New Acquaintance
tropes.html: When Bryan finds out that Kim has a new boyfriend named Jamie, the first thing he does is run a background check on the latter... just as he did with all her other previous boyfriends. Lenore tells him to not run a background check on Jamie, because she knows that he ALWAYS does this.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: Suko stabs Jean-Claude's genitals with scissors to torture him.

tropes.name: Hot Pursuit
tropes.html: Lampshaded. Bryan had to shoot a cop just to ensure that Kim and himself could even get away from the bad guys' hideout, and he flat-out says it. On top of that, the cab they were driving was stolen.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: The Albanians want revenge on Bryan for killing their relatives and friends, and are totally unwilling to accept said relatives' own responsibility for the countless families they ruined in conducting their sex slavery operation, not to mention the fact that Bryan's actions were motivated by the exact same behavior the Albanians condemn him for.

tropes.name: I Did What I Had to Do
tropes.html: Both Bryan and Kim end up committing numerous criminal offenses throughout Istanbul just to get Lenore back.Examples includeDitching a taxi cab without paying the cabbie, then stealing it; throwing hand grenades in a populated area (albeit at targets that are definitely unoccupied); shooting a police officer and evading the police; and, lastly, numerous counts of property damage. They were in the heat of the moment, so they didn't have much time to think about what they're doing. Nearly all of this would typically be handled by the US Embassy and they'd get off without much hassle, but Bryan has to call his buddy Sam to pull some strings at the embassy just to make sure the US military doesn't shoot them as they barrel their way inside.note The ground that embassies are built on is officially deemed part of its country. Any crimes committed by a US citizen in a US Embassy would be prosecuted as if they were committed stateside. Nearly killing US soldiers on US soil definitely counts.

tropes.name: I Have Your Wife
tropes.html: Technically, she's his ex-wife, but the trope still applies.

tropes.name: Impaled with Extreme Prejudice
tropes.html: Murad ends up hanging by a towel hook impaled in his brain stem.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
Murad's funeral speech in the Villain Opening Scene parallels Bryan's quote-worthy threat from the first movie, especially the "I will find you" part.
Murad: He slaughtered our men, our brothers, our sons. The dead cry out to us... for justice. On their souls, I swear to you. The man who took our loved ones from us, the man who has brought us such pain and sorrow. We will find him. We will bring him here. We will not rest until his blood flows into this very ground. We will have our revenge.

tropes.name: It's All About Me
tropes.html: As Bryan accuses to Murad, the Albanians' motivation for avenging their relatives is not out of a sense of justice (which is what Murad proclaims), but simply because their losses hurt them. For Murad's case, see Moral Myopia below.

tropes.name: It Works Better with Bullets
tropes.html:
• In one of the trope's finest-ever uses, the abductors shoot a random hotel guest.
  • Bryan pulls this trick on Murad.

tropes.name: Last-Second Chance
tropes.html: Bryan tries to offer Murad a chance to walk away in exchange for leaving them in peace. Murad blows it by going for Bryan's discarded gun.

tropes.name: Maybe Ever After
tropes.html: It's implied at the end that Bryan and Lenore will reunite as a couple, but they don't officially do so on screen.

tropes.name: Mexican Standoff
tropes.html: The brief fight with several Albanians that leads up to Bryan and Lenore's kidnapping ends up in this situation for a moment, until another Albanian squad comes in to solve the conflict in the Albanians' favor.

tropes.name: Mirror Character
tropes.html: Two Papa Wolves square off over their children, both of them willing to break laws and endanger others if it gets them what they want.

tropes.name: Moe Greene Special
tropes.html: Bryan performs this on one of the Mooks in the climax with one of the many bullet holes said mook and his partner (who calls him "Mirko") left following a barrage of shots through a wall.

tropes.name: Moral Myopia
tropes.html: Invoked by Murad. Bryan killed his son, and that makes him the bad guy. The fact that Marko was practically a mass murderer to begin with, having condemned an unknown number of girls to a short life of sexual slavery, is irrelevant to the calculations. Murad even cheerfully tells Bryan that he intends to finish Marko's job of selling Kim as a sex slave.

tropes.name: Neck Snap
tropes.html: With many enemies, it looks like they are dying from a simple touch administered by Bryan, thanks to the removal of the crisp "crunching" sound to secure a PG-13 rating.

tropes.name: Newspaper-Thin Disguise
tropes.html: Done by one of the Albanians while he watches after Bryan.

tropes.name: Non-Action Big Bad
tropes.html: Much like his son in the first movie, pistols are the only means of fighting that Murad uses. Plus, arguing with Bryan is all he directly does against him, and he attempts to fight in the wrong time and situation for him.<!--* NotAGame-->

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Bryan makes a deal with Murad to end this war between him and Murad's family. Murad goes back on it and immediately comes to the realization that it was a very bad idea.

tropes.name: The Patriarch
tropes.html: Murad.

tropes.name: Photographic Memory
tropes.html: Bryan takes this trope to truly frightening levels. He was able to trace his steps back to where he and Lenore were held by the kidnappers in spite of being blind-folded on their first ten minute long trip, by remembering the sounds he heard on the way and how far/long the spaces are between each sound. Eek.

tropes.name: Railroad Tracks of Doom
tropes.html: In the car chase scene, the second of two Albanian drivers going after the taxi Kim and Bryan are on is tricked into passing through a railroad track just in time to get crushed by an incoming train.

tropes.name: Red Shirt
tropes.html: The security officers at the hotel.

tropes.name: Revenge Before Reason
tropes.html: Murad was really Bullying a Dragon. Had he quietly restarted the trafficking ring and kept under Bryan's radar rather than seeking vengeance, he might have avoided all this.

tropes.name: Revenge by Proxy
tropes.html: Bryan killed their families? The Albanians will kill his ex-wife and sell his daughter like the last time.

tropes.name: Revenge Myopia
tropes.html:
Murad explicitly says he doesn't care what his son did to invite Bryan's wrath, only that Bryan killed him. Worse yet, he intends to finish what his son started and outright tells this to Bryan, knowing it will more than likely press the latter's Berserk Button.
Bryan: I killed your son because he kidnapped my daughter!
Murad: [slaps Bryan] I DON'T CARE WHAT HE DID! I only know... I will never see his face again, I will never hear his voice. (kisses Marko's photo) And as you held him responsible for your daughter, I hold you responsible for him!

tropes.name: Revised Ending
tropes.html: The film originally had a different ending than the one that ended up in cinemas. In the original ending, Bryan rescues Lenore from Murad's men before going to the Embassy and she is the one who gives Kim directions while Bryan shoots the cars chasing them. They crash into the Embassy, call Sam for help and cuddle as a family while they wait for the all clear. A representative comes to greet them and Bryan introduces Kim and Lenore with an awkward moment because he doesn't know how to describe his and Lenore's relationship. He decides to go after Murad and Lenore follows him, asking what he's going to do. Bryan replies, "What I do best," and turns to go. Lenore watches him leave before turning to comfort Kim. Bryan tracking and fighting Murad and his men is the same as the theatrical version only without Lenore's scenes. After this, the ending continues as it did in the theatrical cut with Kim passing her driving test and them going out for milkshakes with a surprise appearance by Jamie. Olivier Megaton felt that Bryan going after Murad and his men after Lenore and Kim were safe put his actions into a morally grey area that he was uncomfortable with, so he prolonged Lenore's rescue to make Bryan's actions more justifiable.

tropes.name: Right on the Tick
tropes.html: Bryan is giving his daughter a driving lesson at 2 PM and waits in the car until the exact second the clock strikes 2. Averted later on, when he deliberately waits an extra minute.

tropes.name: Roofhopping
tropes.html: Done by Kim and two Albanians coming after her during a rooftop chase scene. One of said Albanians accidentally hits a hanging wire and falls to the ground in his attempt.

tropes.name: Scenery Porn
tropes.html: The shots of Istanbul and the cemetery in Albania.

tropes.name: Secret Test of Character
tropes.html: Bryan administers one to Murad. He fails.

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html:
In spite of Luc Besson claiming that there will be no more Taken movies at the time of Taken 2's release, someone else in the production (likely Olivier Megaton or the executives) HAD to leave an opening for a third movie:
Bryan: You have other sons?
Murad: Two.
  • To be fair about that exchange, though, Bryan immediately points out that he'll kill those two sons too. Whether said third movie would have had the involvement of Besson was another story altogether. Ironically, this hook wasn't followed up on in the actual Taken 3, which ended up having Besson on board once again.

tropes.name: Stuff Blowing Up
tropes.html: Much more so than in the first movie.

tropes.name: Shell-Shocked Veteran
tropes.html: Kim clearly isn't over getting kidnapped in the first movie, and she has a flashback the instant she hears Bryan telling her that he and her mother are going to be taken.

tropes.name: Tap on the Head
tropes.html: Subverted. The final fight is not filled with flashy moves and both sides end up getting really hurt. Suko actually dies because Bryan throws him down and makes him hit his head on a concrete corner.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Badass
tropes.html: Kim reacts rather rationally to the kidnapping of her mother, roofhops in Istanbul, faces an Albanian at gunpoint, performs combat driving that would make Jason Statham wince; and most importantly of all, gaining the courage to rescue her parents alone rather than running to the safety of the American Embassy and letting them die, in spite of not possessing any combat training herself. Only time will tell if she will live up to her father's legacy as a warrior.

tropes.name: Third Time's the Charm
tropes.html: Kim passes her driving test on the third try.

tropes.name: Too Happy to Live
tropes.html: Bryan's family.

tropes.name: Took a Level in Jerkass
tropes.html: Stuart, who helped secure a private flight for Bryan in the first film, abruptly cancels the family spring break trip.

tropes.name: Uncertain Doom
tropes.html:
• Jean-Claude vanishes from the series after this film's scene where the Albanians torture him for information on Bryan's whereabouts. One can only assume that they killed him once they got what they wanted...
  • It's also unclear what happened to Jean-Claude's wife and children.

tropes.name: Unwilling Suspension
tropes.html: In the sequel, Lenore gets put in a painful-looking suspended hogtie by the Albanians. Definitely not the usual Fanservice example for a woman, as she's fully clothed, hooded, and bleeding to death.

tropes.name: Villains Out Shopping
tropes.html: In one of the rooms where the Albanians operate at, several members are initially seen watching a soccer match on television while eating and drinking. They prefer to keep doing that when Murad notifies them that he's going outside due to the trackers being unable to find Kim. Bryan later shows up just in time to interrupt their fun with a fight.

tropes.name: Villains Want Mercy
tropes.html: Murad after failing Bryan's Secret Test of Character, subtly enough. His feared expression had "plead for mercy" written all over it. Bryan doesn't give the bastard time to beg for his life and kills him.

tropes.name: Watching the Sunset
tropes.html: Watching the Sunset

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Mook?
tropes.html: While Bryan kills or knocks out most of the Albanian Mooks without mercy, he offers Murad a second chance in their post-climactic confrontation.

tropes.name: You Killed My Father
tropes.html: The villains are motivated by taking revenge on Bryan for killing their relatives (as well as their friends) in the first film. A specific example, aside from Murad's son Marko, is Suko mentioning to Jean-Claude that Bryan killed his brother and an unspecified number of friends.

title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
original_title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
intro: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery is a 1997 American spy comedy film starring Mike Myers and directed by Jay Roach. It is the first installment in the Austin Powers series. The film stars Myers, Elizabeth Hurley, Robert Wagner, Seth Green, and Michael York. Swinging 1960s superspy Austin Powers is cryogenically frozen and thawed out in the 1990s to stop his nemesis Dr. Evil. Followed by

tropes.name: Above the Influence
tropes.html: Austin, for all his womanizing, turns down a kiss (and probably more) from Vanessa because she's drunk.

tropes.name: Academy of Evil
tropes.html: The evil medical school Dr. Evil went to.

tropes.name: Arson, Murder, and Jaywalking
tropes.html: While snooping around Alotta Fagina's penthouse, Austin discovers a folder with some of Virtucon's Evil Plans listed inside. In between "Human Organ Trafficking" and "Project Vulcan" is... "Carrot Top Movie".

tropes.name: Artistic License – Geology
tropes.html:
A pretty minor example: Dr. Evil refers to the Earth's core as the "liquid-hot magma core". The Earth's innermost core is a mass of iron and nickel, solidified by the intense pressure around it. Though Dr. Evil might be referring to the outer core, which is liquid.
  • Even if Austin hadn't been able to stop the bomb from going off, it would not have happened anyway since the heat in the outer core, which can reach almost 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit, would have long-since melted the detonation devices into useless clumps of slag and the warhead would have just melted, provided the extreme temperatures didn't cause the drill itself to melt.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Linguistics
tropes.html: Alotta Fajina's last name is pronoucned phonetically as "fah-gy-na" but since she is Italian, it should be pronounced "fah-jee-na".

tropes.name: Artistic License – Physics
tropes.html: The Big Boy rocket begins to glow from re-entry the instant it begins to move downwards. But that glow is caused by compression heating which increases with the density of the atmosphere you're falling through at extreme altitudes it would still have a small effect and outside the atmosphere it does not occur at all.

tropes.name: Bathroom Brawl
tropes.html: Austin fights the assassin Patty O'Brian when the latter ambushes him in the restroom. A man outside the stalls overhears Austin grunting "Who does Number Two work for?" and assumes he's just constipated.

tropes.name: Behind the Black
tropes.html: Vanessa and Austin walk down a corridor. Random Task steps out from behind a filing cabinet and smashes their heads together - but they should have seen him as they passed by it.

tropes.name: Big Red Button
tropes.html: Two of them. One aborts the underground drill carrying the nuke, the other activates the base's Self-Destruct Mechanism.

tropes.name: Blind People Wear Sunglasses
tropes.html: When Austin enters a casino bathroom, the bathroom attendant is wearing dark glasses. When Austin sees this, he concludes that the man is blind.

tropes.name: Bowdlerise
tropes.html:
• Some TV edits omit any use of "horny". So Austin's infamous "Do I make you horny, baby?" sounds like this instead:
Austin: Do I make you randy? Randy? Do I make you randy, baby?
  • Other TV edits changed "Allota Fagina" to "Allota Cleavage," pronounced "cleave-va-jay," which some have pointed out isn't any less dirty than the original. Tellingly, modern rebroadcasts retain the original name.

tropes.name: Brain Bleach
tropes.html: "Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day! Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day!"

tropes.name: Bread, Eggs, Milk, Squick
tropes.html: One blue crushed velvet suit, one lacey cravat, one medallion with male symbol, one pair of Italian boots, one vinyl record, "Burt Bacharach Plays His Hits", one Swedish-made penis enlarger pump...

tropes.name: Bring My Brown Pants
tropes.html: When Vanessa asks Austin for his plan to escape the mutated sea bass, Austin replies, "First, I plan to soil myself. Then I'm going to regroup and come up with a new plan. Any thoughts?"

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• The Swedish-made penis enlarger pump which belongs to no one in particular and certainly not Austin proves to be a surprisingly effective weapon against Random Task.
  • While Austin is being shown gadgets, Vanessa also shows him toothpaste, dental floss and mouthwash- the gag is that none of them are disguised weapons, she just was trying to politely get him to improve his dental hygiene. However, the floss and toothpaste actually do come in handy to escape a death trap later on.

tropes.name: Cold Water Quells Libido
tropes.html: Austin, in bed cuddling with multiple fembots, wakes up and realizes he has to get Dr. Evil. He then starts saying "Baseball, cold showers, Baseball, cold showers" as a way to get his libido down As one of the fembots tells him to give up and starts unzipping, he desperately starts muttering "Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day! Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day!"

tropes.name: Collapsing Lair
tropes.html: Played with, of course, when Dr. Evil's lair explodes; the actual explosion is shown through grainy old Stock Footage.

tropes.name: Comically Missing the Point
tropes.html:
Vanessa: Well, did you use protection?
Austin: Of course. I had my 9mm automatic.
Vanessa: You know I meant 'did you use a condom'?
Austin: No. Only sailors use condoms, baby.
Vanessa: Not in the '90s, Austin.
Austin: Well they should, those filthy buggers, they go from port to port.

tropes.name: Cosmopolitan Council
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's Council and also, the United Nations have a wide variety of cultures and ethnicities present.

tropes.name: Countrystan
tropes.html: Played for Laughs. Dr. Evil's forces steal a nuclear warhead from a breakaway Russian republic called Kreplachistan. Kreplach are a type of dumpling.

tropes.name: Crazy Memory
tropes.html:
Dr. Evil describes his father as this.
Dr. Evil: He would make outrageous claims, like he invented the question mark.

tropes.name: Crystal Clear Picture
tropes.html: Parodied when, during the 1960s, Austin receives a video call in a car that uses the post-production overlay effect to show a very clear picture, as was often done in films of that era. When Austin is in the 1990s, he has another video conversation via a computer that is presented realistically with the technology of the time, leaving Austin baffled by the lower image quality and framerate.

tropes.name: Cut Lex Luthor a Check
tropes.html: Played for laughs. When Dr. Evil comes out of cryogenic suspension, he immediately draws up outlandish plans to blackmail world leaders for one million dollars. This annoys Number Two to no end, since he has spent the thirty years Dr. Evil was absent building up the front companies they established into a shady but completely law-abiding, legitimate and wildly successful corporation with an annual revenue of nine billion dollars.

tropes.name: Death Trap
tropes.html:
Parodied, of course.
Dr. Evil: No Scott, I have a better idea. I'm going to place him in an easily escapable situation involving an overly elaborate and exotic death... [Beat] ...what?

tropes.name: Deer in the Headlights
tropes.html: Parodied with the guard and the steamroller.

tropes.name: Deliberate Values Dissonance
tropes.html: The movie gets a number of jokes about The '60s and The '90s being different decades with different social mores. Austin ends up declaring that the actual acts of liberal drug use and sex of the sixties wasn't just about liberal drug use and sex for the sake of having those things, it was about freedom, and expressing and enjoying that freedom, a spirit that lives on strong in the nineties.

tropes.name: Didn't Think This Through
tropes.html: This is what gets Number Two killed in the climax (at least until his resurrection in the next film). Number Two seats himself at Dr. Evil’s conference table, intending to negotiate with Austin. Therein lies Number Two’s mistake: he’s seated himself at a conference table where (as he should know from 30 years of experience) every single seat is rigged to dump its occupant into the fire pit beneath the floor. And Dr. Evil, who he's betraying, is currently being held at gunpoint on the other side of the table and is mere inches from the kill switch.

tropes.name: Disguised in Drag
tropes.html:
One of Dr. Evil's assassins disguises himself as a waitress at the club that Austin and Mrs. Kensington go to. Austin sees right through it.
Mrs. Kensington: Austin, why on Earth did you punch that woman?
Austin: That's not a woman. It's a man, man. [pulls off the hat and wig]

tropes.name: Does This Remind You of Anything?
tropes.html:
Dr. Evil's warhead.
Austin: Does that make you horny?
Vanessa: Not now, Austin!

tropes.name: Early-Installment Weirdness
tropes.html: Despite all of the goofy comedy, the film is more straightforward as a parody of 60's Bond films. It even features some suprisingly-poignant personality growth for Austin himself, who, being confronted with the realities of the world he wakes up in and his fledgling relationship with Vanessa, slowly changes into a more mature version of himself. Nearly all of this is ejected for the sequels, which choose instead to focus on a more Denser and Wackier approach, fourth wall breaking, and LOTS of self-deprecation and toilet humor.

tropes.name: Elaborate Underground Base
tropes.html:
Dr. Evil has one.
Dr. Evil: Welcome to my UNDERGROUND LAIR!!

tropes.name: Even Mooks Have Loved Ones
tropes.html: A few scenes (which were cut from the American release, but included in most international ones) are cutaways about the friends and loved ones of guards Austin kills being informed: one with friends at his bachelor party wondering why he's late, and the other his girlfriend and her son (who considers the guard a substitute father figure).

tropes.name: Exposed Embarrassing Purchase
tropes.html:
The Swedish Penis Enlarger Pump, though in this case he'd already bought it and wasn't in a store. His embarrassment isn't helped by the fact that he kept all the purchase information... or that he apparently wrote a book about how much he loves it.
Clerk: [giving Austin back his items] One Swedish-made penis enlarger pump.
Austin: (to Vanessa, embarrassed) That's not mine.
Clerk: One credit card receipt for Swedish-made penis enlarger signed by Austin Powers.
Austin: I'm telling ya, baby, that's not mine!
Clerk: One warranty card for Swedish-made penis enlarger pump, filled out by Austin Powers.
Austin: I don't even know what this is! This sort of thing ain't my bag, baby!
Clerk: One book, Swedish-Made Penis Enlargers and Me (This Sort of Thing Is My Bag, Baby). By Austin Powers.
Austin: (stunned) ...Ah.
Clerk: Just sign the form.

tropes.name: The Faceless
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's face is never seen in the beginning of the film. It is finally seen after he burns Mustafa alive and says, "Let this be a lesson to you all that this organization will not tolerate failure," revealing that the villain of the movie is also played by Mike Myers.

tropes.name: Failed Future Forecast
tropes.html: In-universe Austin, after being frozen in 1967 and unfrozen in 1997, is shocked at the presence of a Russian intelligence officer. When he is told that the Cold War ended, he initially assumes that the Communists won.

tropes.name: Fetal Position Rebirth
tropes.html: Austin Powers adopts this position when he's unfrozen.

tropes.name: Fiendish Fish
tropes.html: Played for Laughs. Dr. Evil asked his henchmen for a Shark Pool with Frickin' Laser Beams attached to their heads, but they had to settle for "ill-tempered mutant seabass". He gets his wish in later movies, however.

tropes.name: Fish out of Temporal Water
tropes.html:
Austin and Dr. Evil have to face the changes arisen from being frozen 30 years. Which includes:
  • Two plots Dr. Evil cooked up in the 60's have already happened in the 90's. He's too late to the punch to damage the ozone layer and his Royal Family sex scandal plot won't work because there already was a Royal Family sex scandal.
  • Austin's swinging lifestyle and velvet suits are no longer in fashion in the 90's and he now comes off as weird instead of hip.
  • Both of them being deeply confused by modern technology and culture.

tropes.name: Flipping the Bird
tropes.html: Mini-Me's favorite method of insult, most often given to Scott and Austin.

tropes.name: For the Evulz
tropes.html: Near the end, Dr. Evil cheerfully informs Austin that, even if the world pays his $100 billion ransom, he's still going to set off the bomb and trigger a global geological catastrophe, because eeeeevil. Of course, this would render his ill-gotten gains completely worthless, since after such a cataclysm there wouldn't be an economy left, but this is right on-brand for him.

tropes.name: Grossout Fakeout
tropes.html: Several variants of this trope were used in the trilogy; most notably Austin's fight in a toilet stall with O'Brien in the first film (the man in the stall next to him thinks Austin is constipated), and the two "silhouette gags" in the latter two movies (a scene with Austin and Felicity in a tent in the second film makes it look like Felicity is preforming a series of Ass Shoves, while in the third film Austin and Mini-Me are behind a privacy screen and make it look like Austin has a Gag Penis).

tropes.name: Gross-Up Close-Up
tropes.html:
One of the scene transitions ends with a close-up of Austin's bad teeth for no reason.
  • The fact that Ms. Kensington had brought it up immediately before the transition isn't a reason?

tropes.name: Hazmat Suit
tropes.html: The radiation suit Dr. Evil wears is a parody of the one worn by the title character in Dr. No.

tropes.name: Hook Hand
tropes.html: Don Luigi, one of the assassins who Dr. Evil executes for failing to kill Austin Powers, has one of these. He uses it to smoke cigars.

tropes.name: Human Popsicle
tropes.html: Austin and Dr. Evil.

tropes.name: Hypocrite
tropes.html: Dr. Evil shows no care for Scott whatsoever when Austin takes him hostage, and tells him to his face that he had the father/son group "liquidated". Yet when Scott tells his father he hates him, Dr. Evil claims that it hurt his feelings.

tropes.name: I Have Your Wife
tropes.html: Though Austin hadn't married Vanessa yet at this point, Alotta Fagina takes Vanessa hostage when Austin is on the verge of bringing Dr. Evil to justice. This gives Dr. Evil a chance to escape, despite the failed insurrection by Number Two and Vanessa knocking Alotta out and escaping with Austin.

tropes.name: Implausible Deniability
tropes.html: Austin's increasingly desperate insistence that "Swedish-Made Penis Enlarger Pump" wasn't his bag, baby, as the evidence continued to mount against him.

tropes.name: Inflation Negation
tropes.html: One meeeeeeeee-llion dollar ransom. Memetic Mutation as well. This was so ubiquitous, even King Hussein of Jordan joked around with it.

tropes.name: Instantly Proven Wrong
tropes.html:
Austin is repeatedly called out for his ownership of a Swedish penis-enlarger pump while he's picking up his belongings after the unfreezing process. This embarrasses him in front of Vanessa Kensington and causes him to resort to Implausible Deniability.
Clerk: One Swedish-made penis enlarger pump...
Austin: That's not mine.
Clerk: One credit card receipt for Swedish-made penis enlarger, signed by... Austin Powers.
Austin: [to Vanessa] I'm telling you, baby, that's not mine.
Clerk: One warranty card for Swedish-made penis enlarger pump, filled out by... Austin Powers.
Austin: I don't even know what this is. This sort of thing ain't my bag, baby.
Clerk: One book: Swedish-made Penis Enlarger Pumps and Me: (This Sort of Thing Is My Bag, Baby), by... Austin Powers.
Austin: Ah.

tropes.name: Intimate Artistry
tropes.html: Austin was flirting with Vanessa from the very instant that he awoke from his cryogenic freezing, but he only seemed to progress from purely-physical attraction to an emotional connection when she briefly posed for photographs for him when they were on a surveillance mission. After saying how beautiful she was he took her out for a night on the town, where she first began to return his affections.

tropes.name: Inventor of the Mundane
tropes.html: During a group therapy session Dr. Evil mentions that his father claimed to have invented the question mark (among many other, equally strange declarations).

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html: See Instantly Proven Wrong above.

tropes.name: It's Been Done
tropes.html:
When he's unfrozen, Dr. Evil suggests evil plans that are moot because they've already happened (ruining Prince Charles's marriage, punching a hole in the ozone layer).
Dr. Evil: Right, people, you have to tell me these things, okay? I've been frozen for thirty years, okay? Throw me a frickin' bone here!

tropes.name: Just a Gangster
tropes.html: When Dr. Evil is unfrozen, he insists on bringing his organization back to its old ways despite the fact that it has become much more successful and lucrative as a legitimate business.

tropes.name: Just in Time
tropes.html: Played for laughs. Austin has well over ten seconds to stop Dr. Evil's drill from reaching the Earth's core, but deliberately waits until there's just a second to spare, so that his Big "NO!" will look more dramatic.

tropes.name: Kavorka Man
tropes.html:
Despite his lecherous behavior, yellow, crooked teeth, and general lack of game, woman still seem ridiculously attracted to him. Lampshaded by Mrs. Kensington telling Vanessa more about Austin.
Mrs. Kensington:In the sixties, you could be a sex symbol and still have bad teeth. It didn't matter!

tropes.name: Kirk Summation
tropes.html:
Austin's response to Dr. Evil's "Not So Different" Remark attempt.
Austin: I've got you, Dr. Evil!
Dr. Evil: Well done, Mr. Powers. We're not so different, you and I. It's true, you're British, and I'm Belgian. You have a full head of hair, mine is slightly receding. You're thin, I'm about forty pounds overweight. OK, we are different, I'm not making a very good point. However, isn't it ironic, Mr. Powers, that the very things you stand for: swinging, free love, parties, distrust of authority- are all now, in The '90s, considered to be... evil? Maybe we have more in common than you care to admit.
Austin: No, man, what we swingers were rebelling against were uptight squares like you, whose bag was money and world domination. We were innocent, man. If we'd known the consequences of our sexual liberation, we would have done things differently, but the spirit would have remained the same. It's freedom, man.
Dr. Evil: Your freedom has caused more pain and suffering in the world than any plan I ever dreamed of. Face it, freedom failed.
Austin: No, man, freedom didn't fail. Right now, we've got freedom and responsibility.

tropes.name: Lame Rhyme Dodge
tropes.html:
Dr. Evil: Son, wouldn't you like to see what daddy does for a living?
Scott Evil: Blow me.
Dr. Evil: What?
Scott Evil: Show me.
(The TV edited version works just as well:)
Dr. Evil: Son, wouldn't you like to see what daddy does for a living?
Scott Evil: Bite me.
Dr. Evil: What?
Scott Evil: Might be... fun.

tropes.name: Low-Speed Chase
tropes.html: Austin and Vanessa try to escape pursuing guards in a steamroller that moves so slowly that the guards should be able to easily catch up to them.

tropes.name: Mission Creep
tropes.html: Parodied. The defrosted Dr. Evil returning from The '60s to The '90s tries to launch into an old-fashioned spy supervillain plot only to be reminded that his organization in his absence had to Cut Lex Luthor a Check and branch into legitimate corporate enterprise so as to better serve evil of course.

tropes.name: Mistaken for an Imposter
tropes.html: "That's not your mother, it's a MAN, Baby!... WHY! WON'T this WIG! come OFF!"

tropes.name: Mugged for Disguise
tropes.html: Subverted and parodied. When Austin and Vanessa are infiltrating Virtucon, they notice an extremely heavyset female scientist and a thin, lanky scientist almost seven feet tall go into the restrooms; they follow them, and emerge wearing a pair of perfectly-fitting uniforms. They also do this right in front of the tour guide, who alerts the guards, making the whole charade pointless.

tropes.name: Naked People Are Funny
tropes.html: There's two Overly Long Gags in which Austin and latter Vanessa make full use of Scenery Censor.

tropes.name: Newspaper-Thin Disguise
tropes.html: Austin attempts to disguise himself with a magazine... with his own face on the cover.

tropes.name: Next Stall Shenanigans
tropes.html:
Austin's visit to the can is interrupted by an assassin, who he eventually overpowers and drowns in the toilet. While this is going on, the guy in the next stall is keeping a running commentary on what he's hearing.
*Austin puts the assassin head-first into the toilet*
Austin: Who does Number Two work for?!
Other guy: That's right, buddy, you show that turd who's boss!
[the assassin starts noisily drowning]
Other guy: Hey, uh, that sounds pretty nasty. How about a courtesy flush over there?

tropes.name: NO INDOOR VOICE
tropes.html: "I'm finding it hard to control THE VOLUME OF MY VOICE!"

tropes.name: No, Mr. Bond, I Expect You to Dine
tropes.html:
Lampshaded and spoofed.
Scott: What, you're feeding him? Why don't you just kill him?

tropes.name: No-Nonsense Nemesis
tropes.html:
Scott Evil is outraged by his daddy Dr. Evil's dogged insistence on Bond Villain Stupidity by having dinner with his arch-enemy Austin Powers and deciding to place him in an easily escapable Death Trap. Scott offers to just shoot the super-spy and be done with it, but Dr. Evil simply ignores him.
Dr. Evil: Scott... you just don't get it.

tropes.name: Outfit-Rip Sex Check
tropes.html:
• Early in the film Powers grabs a pretty mod girl and declares "it's a man, man!" and pulls her wig off, revealing a male spy.
  • Later in the film, Powers meets Basil Exposition's mother and he thinks it's another male spy in a little old lady disguise, but it turns out this one really is a little old lady.

tropes.name: Overly Long Gag
tropes.html:
so frequent it’s also a Running Gag but we have:
  • Austin’s “evacuation” after being thawed from cryogenic freezing.
  • Austin‘s attempts to deny that the Swedish penis enlarger is his.
  • Mustafa being Not Quite Dead after being cast into the incinerator.
  • the guard's Big "NO!" at the steamroller slowly approaching him.
  • Austin attempting to turn the cart around in a narrow hallway.

tropes.name: Overly Long Scream
tropes.html:
Parodied. A Mook lets off a few loud Big "NO!" screams, one after another, as a steamroller is about to crush him. This is despite the fact that he's several yards away from the steamroller, which is going so slowly that the mook could just walk to escape it.
"NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!!!! NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!!!!!! NOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOO!!! NOOOOOOOAAAAAHHHHH-" [steamroller runs him over]

tropes.name: People Jars
tropes.html: There is a cryogenic storage facility with frozen celebrities in pods. Amongst them Vanilla Ice◊.

tropes.name: Planetary Core Manipulation
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's nefarious plot is to use a "big underground drill" to penetrate the Earth's crust and plant a 50 kiloton nuclear warhead deep in the core of the planet. When the bomb detonates, every volcano on Earth will erupt simultaneously.

tropes.name: Player Nudge
tropes.html:
The blackjack dealer at the casino does this twice.
  • The first time, he advises Number Two against hitting on 17. Number Two ignores this, saying, "I like to live dangerously." Unbeknownst to the dealer, Number Two used the X-ray vision from his eyepatch to see that his next card will put him at 21.
  • The second time, Austin wants to stay on 5. The dealer tells Austin to hit, but Austin says, "I also like to live dangerously." The dealer easily beats Austin's 5 with 20.

tropes.name: Pop-Cultural Osmosis Failure
tropes.html: Patty O'Brian can't understand why people keep laughing when he says Interpol are "after [his] lucky charms".

tropes.name: Post-Climax Confrontation
tropes.html: At the end during Austin and Vanessa's honeymoon, Random Task shows up again to kill them... and is defeated with the help of the penis enlargement pump.

tropes.name: Punctuated!  For!  Emphasis!
tropes.html: "DO! YOU! WORK! FOR! NUMBER! TWO!??" (original release version. The current releases use the clip of Austin shouting "Who... does... Number Two... work for?!")

tropes.name: Punny Name
tropes.html: According to the invokedDVD Commentary, the Sphynx cat playing Mr. Bigglesworth was called Ted Nude-Gent.

tropes.name: Put Their Heads Together
tropes.html: As Austin and Vanessa are infiltrating Virtucon, Random Task comes up behind them and cracks their heads together, knocking them out.

tropes.name: Pyrrhic Victory
tropes.html: When Austin catches Dr. Evil attempting to escape after Austin stopped the nuclear warhead, Dr. Evil attempts to impose this on Austin. He argues that free love and anything Austin stood up for in the 1960's is considered "evil", but Austin argues that they aren't and he's come to understand how much the world changed but can be similar motives adapted for the 1990's, saying "It's freedom, baby, Yeah!" Dr. Evil is still smug that even though Austin has caught him, Dr. Evil says "Freedom failed" and Austin would be forced to live with all that, and not in a good way. Luckily for Dr. Evil, Alotta Fagina arrives holding Vanessa hostage. This gives Dr. Evil a chance to escape after a failed intervention by Number Two.

tropes.name: Rank Up
tropes.html: At the end of the movie, Basil informs Vanessa that she's been made a full agent.

tropes.name: Rip Van Tinkle
tropes.html: Austin's epic urination after being awakened from cryo-sleep.

tropes.name: Sealed Evil in a Can
tropes.html: The freezing of Dr. Evil.

tropes.name: Sealed Good in a Can
tropes.html: The freezing of Austin.

tropes.name: Self-Destruct Mechanism
tropes.html: Dr. Evil's underground base in the first film and moon base in the second one has them. Which can causes the bases to, well, self-destruct.

tropes.name: Sexophone
tropes.html: When Austin first encounters the Fembots, saxophone music plays.

tropes.name: Sexy Silhouette
tropes.html: Alotta Fagina undresses behind a semi-transparent wall, causing Austin's libido to go crazy more than usual.

tropes.name: Shoe Slap
tropes.html: Random Task throws his shoe, as a parody of Oddjob's doing the same with his hat.

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html: The "Really, there's nothing more pathetic than an aging hipster" line is a reference to Lenny Bruce saying "There's nothing sadder than an aging hipster."

tropes.name: Standard Snippet
tropes.html: George S. Clinton's arrangement of "Rule, Britannia!" as Commander Gilmour is summoned to London.

tropes.name: Suddenly Obvious Fakery
tropes.html: Played for laughs. Austin is in a nightclub on the lookout for Dr. Evil's assassins when he suddenly punches an attractive woman. When he removes "her" wig, the assassin is suddenly and very obviously a burly, unshaven stunt artist in drag.

tropes.name: Swirlie
tropes.html: Austin drowns Patty O'Brien in a hotel toilet.

tropes.name: A Taste of Their Own Medicine
tropes.html: The Fembots were designed to seduce men so they could kill them. Austin uses the power of his mojo to cause them to overload and explode through sheer desire.

tropes.name: That Makes Me Feel Angry
tropes.html: Dr. Evil: That makes me angry. And when Dr. Evil gets angry, Mr. Bigglesworth gets upset. And when Mr. Bigglesworth gets upset... people DIE!

tropes.name: Think Unsexy Thoughts
tropes.html: To resist the fembots, Austin pictures the least arousing things he can think of, including: baseball, taking a cold shower, and "Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day".

tropes.name: Threatening Shark
tropes.html: Dr. Evil requested that Number 2 provide him with a pool of sharks with "frickin' laser beams attached to their heads". (But he has to do with ill-tempered mutant sea bass. The sharks are an endangered species and too much of a hassle.)

tropes.name: Twinkle Smile
tropes.html: At the end while he's in bed with Vanessa Kensington, Austin does this to show he's embraced dental hygiene.

tropes.name: Twister Game Hijinks
tropes.html: When Austin and Vanessa are in a hotel room together, one scene starts with them hidden behind a sofa. Based on what they're saying to each other, they're apparently having sex. As the camera moves forward to show them, it's revealed that they're actually playing a game of Twister.

tropes.name: Two-Person Pool Party
tropes.html: Austin and Alotta Fagina share a hot tub, spoofing a similar scene from A View to a Kill.

tropes.name: Underwater Fart Gag
tropes.html:
During the hot tub scene, Austin farts.
Alotta: How dare you break wind before me!
Austin: I'm sorry, baby, I didn't know it was your turn!

tropes.name: Uranus Is Showing
tropes.html: Austin makes this joke at the end of the movie.

tropes.name: Video Call Fail
tropes.html: After giving the world his ransom demands, Dr. Evil can't figure out the remote control and inadvertently changes the live feed to Beavis and Butt-Head briefly before ending the transmission.

tropes.name: Weather-Control Machine
tropes.html: Dr. Evil mentions that in the 1960's, he had a "weather changing machine that was, in essence, a sophisticated heat beam, which we called a laser."

tropes.name: What Are Records?
tropes.html: Inverted, with Austin trying to play a CD on a turntable.

tropes.name: What Measure Is a Mook?
tropes.html: Mocked in the extended version of International Man of Mystery. We see the family of the dead guard that Austin smashes with the steamroller learning of his death; later, "John Smith", the guard who gets decapitated, by the "ill tempered mutated sea bass," is shown to have been a day away from marriage, and was late for his bachelor party, because he was working late. In both cases, the families and friends are fully aware, that the mook is a henchman of Dr. Evil, and act like it's just a normal job.

tropes.name: Why Don't You Just Shoot Him?
tropes.html: Scott asks this almost verbatim: "why don't you just kill him?", and offers to shoot Austin himself. (Dr.Evil instead lowers Austin and Vanessa into a pool of mutated sea bass.)

tropes.name: You Have Failed Me
tropes.html: Dr. Evil punishes his minions by dumping them through a trapdoor to be burned alive. After being thawed, Dr. Evil is angry that Mr. Bigglesworth is now devoid of fur, blaming this on Mustafa. As punishment, Mustafa gets dumped into the furnace below; he survives, but he's "very badly burned". Shortly thereafter, he's shot by another mook whose first shot registers a non-lethal hit, but gets the kill with the second. His botched execution is Played for Laughs.

tropes.name: You Just Told Me
tropes.html: Subverted. Austin tricks Alotta Fagina, into admitting her boss is into "big underground drills," but he knew already, and did this to look suave. Counts as a spoof as well, since he is the one who brought up the drills, so he obviously already knew.

tropes.name: Your Head A-Splode
tropes.html: This happens to one of the Fembots during Austin's striptease.

tropes.name: Zoomed-Out Reframing Gag
tropes.html: Austin scatters a team of guards while driving a steamroller, except one who can't get out of the way and screams "No!!!" as the steamroller bears in on him. Then the camera pans out to show that the steamroller is about thirty yards away, the steamroller is moving at a speed of inches an hour and he has plenty of time to get out of its path. Instead he just stands there screaming "No!" until the steamroller finally flattens him.

title: Austin Powers in Goldmember
intro: Austin Powers in Goldmember is a 2002 American spy comedy film starring Mike Myers and directed by Jay Roach. It is the third installment in the Austin Powers film series. The film stars Myers, Beyoncé, Seth Green, Michael York, Robert Wagner, Mindy Sterling, Verne Troyer, and Michael Caine. Austin teams up with Dr. Evil to stop the flamboyant villain Goldmember and rescue his father.

tropes.name: And the Adventure Continues
tropes.html: Scott becomes the new Dr. Evil, and is apparently slightly more crazy, meaning the Powers family will have many more adventures to come.

tropes.name: Antagonist Title
tropes.html: Being a spoof of the Bond movies, Goldmember is used in place of Goldfinger as the title. Goldmember is indeed the antagonist, just not the only one.

tropes.name: Artistic License – Sports
